### Measuring: lanes, stopwatches, tapes, scales and gauges
Instruments read the run and show their reading on their own face every frame (a stopwatch's LCD, a light gate's and a speed sign's LEDs, a kitchen scale's grams, a spring scale's pointer); after a run each one's readings are listed with the item. Their faces, painted lines, tapes, trails and boards touch nothing (display only); the spring scale's hook, the kitchen scale's platform, the pan balance and the gram masses are real things. LINKS are props naming another item by its id: stopwatch.watch (what it times), stopwatch.start_line / finish_line (a start-line, a finish-line or a lane: a lane's finish is its finish_at mark), measuring-tape.watch (whose front it reads), speed-gate.watch (+ pair: an earlier gate, to time between them), speedometer.watch, spring-scale.hook (the thing hung on its hook by a string), protractor.watch (a ramp, pendulum or lever), motion-trail.watch, graph-board.watch/watch2/watch3 (lines), data-table.watch…watch4 (instruments whose readings it lists). A lane is a long floor 1-60 m (a static board 2 cm thick) with a mark every metre (or as set), big upright metre numbers, a white start line at start_at and a chequered finish line at finish_at; its anchor is its 0 m mark on its top surface, so the d-metre mark is at x = lane.x + d and things race on y = lane.y. Two lanes one above the other (y 0.02 and 0.82, the upper one stands on legs) compare two racers without them meeting. Stopwatch: start = release (the scene's release) | moves (the watched thing has moved 1 mm) | crosses (its front reaches start_line or start_x); stop = crosses (its front reaches finish_line or stop_x) | stops (it comes to rest) | hits (it first touches something new) | at (stop_at seconds after the start) | reads (the watched thing's reading stop_reading reaches stop_value, from the side it started on: a sand timer runs out, hourglass empty 1; ice melts, ice-cube melted 1; a thermometer's reading reaches 50; a candle goes out, flame 0; a balloon pops, popped 1; any reading the thing has) | never. It reads to 0.01 s; meters = how far the thing moved while it ran. counts lesson: its face shows the lesson clock (the run's seconds × the time-lapse) and a reads goal's seconds are that. face_cm sets how big its face is drawn (a real one is 6 cm; 30-40 cm reads in a wide 12 m shot). A kitchen-scale also weighs sand heaped on its platform (granular: a funnel above it, a sand-pile on it) and liquid lying on it as a puddle (flow: a tap or a pitcher spilling onto it), at about 1 g a mL of water; what falls on it pushes it only as it rests there (a stream's own push is not added). Readings: stopwatch seconds, meters, start_s, stop_s (lesson_s with counts lesson); measuring-tape meters (0 to its length; past_end 1 beyond its end); speed-gate speed (= length / blocked time), blocked_s, between_s; speedometer speed, top, mean; spring-scale newtons, grams, over (1: past its range, its hook bottomed out 5 % past full scale); kitchen-scale grams; pan-balance tilt (degrees, right pan down +), heavier (-1 left, 0 level, 1 right), left_g and right_g (what each pan holds); protractor degrees (a ramp's slope from level, a pendulum's turn from hanging straight), swing; motion-sensor distance. Weight and mass: a kitchen-scale and a spring-scale show WEIGHT (their grams are the force ÷ the Earth's 9.81: they are calibrated on Earth), so under settings.gravity moon a 1 kg mass reads 1.62 N and 165 g (1/6), on Mars 3.71 N and 378 g; a pan-balance compares MASSES (both pans feel the same g) and reads the same anywhere: 1 kg balances 1 kg on the Moon too. A pan-balance's pans hang 14 cm either side of its middle under the beam: put a thing IN a pan with place {inside: the balance, x: balance.x - 0.14} (left) or {inside: the balance, x: balance.x + 0.14} (right), gram masses the same (they stack in the pan). It tips 1.5° for each gram of difference, up to its 15° stop (10 g or more), and reads level (heavier 0, |tilt| under 0.5°) within 0.3 g; it settles in a few swings of 2-5 s. A lane has a foam bumper on its far end (end_stop): what races past the finish stops there and stays on the lane. A stopwatch with no watch link that starts at the release and stops at stop_at (or never) is a plain clock; a link that names nothing (a wrong id, itself, the wrong kind of item) is listed in the run's warnings.
  - goal reads {item: an instrument, seconds | meters | mps | newtons | grams | degrees | value, key?, tol?}: the instrument's reading at the end is within tol of the number (a stopwatch's time, a tape's metres, a gate's speed, a scale's grams; any module's instrument by value)
  - goal crosses {item, line (a start-line / finish-line / lane: its finish mark) | x (m), before_s?, after_s?}: the thing's front reaches that line (within the times)
  - goal faster {a, b, line? | x?}: a is faster than b (gets to the line, or over the same distance, sooner)
  - goal farther {a, b}: a ends at least 1 cm farther along +x from where it started than b
  - goal stops_between {item, x0, x1}: the thing's middle ends between x0 and x1 (m)
  - knob motor-car.speed: a motor car's top speed (m/s): faster crosses a line sooner and goes farther in the same seconds (time = distance / speed; it drives about 1.6 % under the setting)
  - knob motor-car.push: how hard its motor pushes (N): more gets it up to speed sooner, up to what its tyres can grip
  - knob lane.finish_at: where the race ends: a longer race takes longer (change it only when the request leaves the distance open)
  - knob stopwatch.stop_at: for a watch that stops after set seconds: a later stop lets the thing go farther
  - knob speed-gate.beam_height: the beam must cross the thing's body to see it pass
  - knob spring-scale.range: a stiffer spring holds a heavier thing without running off its scale (it stretches 10 cm at full scale)
  - knob kitchen-scale.tare: taring takes off what was on it at the release
  - knob pan-balance.damping: a damped beam settles sooner instead of rocking
  - knob gram-mass.grams: a brass mass's size (1 g to 1 kg, exact): a pan balance levels when both pans hold the same grams; a scale reads it
  - e.g. "Red car goes 10 m in 3 s, blue car 10 m in 4 s; stopwatches show it": two 10 m lanes (y 0.02 and 0.82), a motor-car on each with its front at 0 m (red speed 3.39 m/s, blue 2.54 m/s, start speeds equal to those), a stopwatch per car (watch, finish_line = its lane, face_cm 40) above each lane's finish; goals reads seconds 3 and 4 (tol 0.05) and faster {red, blue}
  - e.g. "Same 3 seconds: which car goes farther?": both stopwatches stop = at, stop_at = 3; red 3.39 m/s reaches 10 m, blue 2.71 m/s reaches 8 m in the same 3 s; a measuring-tape along each lane watching its car (or read the lane's numbers); goal farther {red, blue}
  - e.g. "Two balls race 10 m": soccer balls on 10 m lanes, held at 0 m with a start_speed; a rolling ball slows (air drag, rolling resistance), so 10 m in 3 s needs about 3.74 m/s at the start (12 % above 10/3); reads goals let the search tune it
  - e.g. "A car rolls down a ramp; how far does it go?": a plank ramp on a lane or the table, a toy-car at its top, a measuring-tape with its zero at the ramp's foot watching the car; a higher ramp sends it farther (goal farther between two set-ups)
  - e.g. "Weigh an apple with a newton meter": a spring-scale (range 5 N) on: air with hook = the apple hanging 3 cm under it; it reads about 1.8 N (180 g × 9.81)
  - e.g. "Show that mass is kept when the clay is squashed": a kitchen-scale with the clay ball on its platform; it reads the same grams before and after (reads goal on grams)
  - e.g. "Which is heavier, the stone or the sponge?": a pan-balance with one in each pan (inside the balance at x = balance.x ∓ 0.14); it tips toward the heavier (reads goal on tilt -15 or 15)
  - e.g. "Does a 1 kg mass weigh less on the Moon?": settings.gravity moon (air false); a kitchen-scale with a 1 kg gram-mass on it reads about 165 g (1.62 N: a scale shows weight); a pan-balance with 1 kg in each pan still balances (mass is the same); goals reads grams 165 tol 2 and reads tilt 0 tol 1
  - e.g. "Measure the ramp's angle": a protractor at the ramp's foot with watch = the ramp; it reads the slope in degrees
  - e.g. "Time a ball dropped from 1 m": a ball held at y 1 m, a stopwatch watch = the ball, start = release, stop = hits: about 0.45 s (√(2h/g))
  - e.g. "Show a speed-time graph of the car": a graph-board behind the scene, plot = speed, watch = the car
  - e.g. "Time a one-minute sand timer with a stopwatch": an hourglass on the table (its 66 g of fine sand run out in about 60 s), settings.time_lapse 4 and seconds 20 (the run shows a lesson minute in 15 s), a stopwatch with watch = the hourglass, start = release, stop = reads (stop_reading empty, stop_value 1), counts lesson; goal reads {item: stopwatch, seconds: 60, tol: 3}
  - e.g. "Weigh the sand a funnel pours onto a kitchen scale": a kitchen-scale on the table and a sand-funnel standing on the table beside it with its spout over the platform (funnel x = scale x; its heap lands on the platform); the scale's grams rise as the heap grows, to the funnel's poured_g (goal reads {item: scale, grams: the funnel's sand_kg × 1000, tol: 5})
### Machines and motion (mechanics): forces, force arrows (free-body diagrams) and energy bars
ANY ITEM (catalog-wide props): color (none, red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, pink, white, black, gray, brown: the look only; a car's or truck's body, not its tyres), glow (true: a soft halo to point it out), and for every moving item start_speed (m/s it already has at the release, a push, kick or launch), start_dir (degrees from the way it faces, counter-clockwise: 0 forward, 180 back, 90 up) and start_spin ("roll": balls and wheels already turning as if rolling). Cars and trucks face right (+x) at angle 0. An egg with props {fragile: true} cracks if it lands hard (peak force over 35 N: about 7 cm or more onto a table breaks it, 80 cm onto a 10 cm foam block does not); goals breaks / survives.
FLOORS, RAMPS, SURFACES: floor (a long ground slab, length up to 60 m, its anchor the middle of its top; material varnished hardwood (gym), concrete, carpet, rubber mat, grass, ice: friction lessons race the same car over different floors). ramp: a plank on `blocks` stacked wooden blocks (5 cm each: blocks 1 vs 3 = rise 5 vs 15 cm), `length` (m), rises "left" (default: the top is length·cos(slope) to the LEFT of its anchor, the foot at the anchor) or "right"; lip true keeps a small stop at the top. A car or cart on a ramp: place {on: <ramp id>, x: the top end + half the car's length + 0.03} (the top end is at the ramp's x − length when it rises left, x + length when it rises right; a 20 cm toy car on a ramp at x 1.0 rising left: x 0.13); it is turned to lie along the slope and rolls down at the release. Put the ramp on the floor item or the table (place {on: <floor id>}); give a floor item an id other than "floor", "ground" or "table" (e.g. "gym-floor"): place.on "floor" means the table. A FAIR TEST of ramp height (1 block vs 3 blocks, the Grade 3 'is this a valid experiment?'): one long carpet floor (length 8: the table alone is too short, its end walls stop the cars), both ramps rising left (the default) so both cars roll right, the 3-block ramp's foot 2.4 m right of the 1-block ramp's (on carpet a toy car rolls about 1 m past a 1-block ramp and 2.5 m past a 3-block one, so the first stops before the second ramp; on wood 3 m and 11 m), the same car (same colour, same clay) on each, only the blocks differ; goal farther {a: the 3-block car, b: the 1-block car} (farther measures the distance along +x).
FORCES AND MOTION: dynamics-cart (a 250 g lab cart: load = kg of bars added, plunger 0-3 = a cocked spring that fires at the release, bumper plain/spring/magnet/velcro/clay: magnet carts bounce apart, velcro and clay stick). puller (a winch on the floor, link pulls = the thing its cord is tied to; mode force: a steady force in N (balanced pulls: two pullers facing each other, equal forces, the cart stays put); faces left/right = the way its cord leaves it; height (3 cm up) = the cord's height: near the pulled thing's middle, the default for a cart; set it 1-2 m away). pusher (a paddle on a rod from a fixed housing: force N for push_time s, a push of F·t that starts a thing of mass m sliding at about F·t/(m + 0.2 kg), or a speed over a stroke; height = the rod's height, the pushed thing's middle: a raised housing stands on its own wooden block; put it left_of the thing with align touching (its paddle's face is 3.2 cm right of its anchor) so the push starts at once; paddle = how tall the paddle is, not how hard it pushes). edge-pulley: clamp it at the table's right end (its anchor = the pulley's axle, place {on: "air", x: the table's right end + 0.04, y_m: 0.016}: the wheel's top level with a dynamics cart's string), link pulls = the cart on the table, hanging_mass falls and pulls it: a = m·g/(M + m) (F = ma; double the cart's mass with load, the acceleration halves). Two carts pushing apart: a plunger cart and a second cart touching its front (left_of/right_of with align touching), the lighter one leaves faster: v_a/v_b = m_b/m_a (goal recoils {a, b, ratio}).
FORCE METERS AND SENSORS (readings in the run, shown in the digest): a puller's `newtons` is the pull in its cord (a force meter); in mode speed it reels in at its set speed, so its reading is the force that takes: pulling a cart UP A RAMP at a steady 0.1 m/s reads m·g·sin(slope), less than lifting it straight up (m·g) (stand the puller on the floor just past the ramp's top end, faces right when the cart is down to its right, its height (the drum's, up to 1 m) on the slope's line there so the cord runs along it). An edge-pulley's `newtons` is the string's pull on the cart (a force sensor: T = M·a, less than the hanging weight). A dynamics-cart reads its own speed (m/s, + forward) and accel (m/s²): F = M·a with the string's pull. Goal pulls_with {item: the puller or edge pulley, newtons, tol?}: its steady reading; measure's reads {item, newtons} reads the end value.
SIMPLE MACHINES (the lever, wheel and axle, block and tackle and gears hang in the air: place {on: "air", y_m}; their stands are drawn; the screw jack stands on the table or floor): lever-kit (class 1, 2 or 3; load kg at load_at m from the fulcrum, effort kg at effort_at m; its masses hang 25 cm under the beam: y_m about 0.6; balances when load × load_at = effort × effort_at, resolved balanced_by says the effort that balances). wheel-and-axle (wheel_radius, axle_radius: MA = R/r; load on the axle's cord, effort on the wheel's; y_m about 1.4 with drop 0.4). block-and-tackle (strands 2-4 = MA; effort = (load + 0.05 kg block) / strands balances; y_m about 1.6). screw-jack (stands on the floor or table: a handle turning a screw lifts a heavy load on its cap a pitch a turn: load kg, effort N at the handle's end, handle m, pitch mm, turns a second, efficiency (0.3); it lifts when efficiency × effort × 2π·handle/pitch > the load's weight: 10 N on a 20 cm handle with a 5 mm thread lifts up to about 75 kg, at 5 mm/s: give the scene seconds 6-10; goal rises {item} (1 cm by default)). gear-train (teeth_a drives at rpm, teeth_b and teeth_c (0 = only two gears): the last gear turns rpm × teeth_a ÷ teeth_last, each pair turning opposite ways; place in the air at a visible height, y_m about 0.5). Goals: balanced {item} (it holds still), rises {item, min_m?} (its load goes up), gear_speed {item, rpm?, direction?} (a gear train's last gear).
ROLLER COASTER (coaster-track: layout curved ramp, valley, hill or loop; height = the start's height (m), size = the loop's radius; its anchor is the floor under the start and it runs to the right). Put the ball (steel-ball, glass-marble) at the start: place {on: <track id>, x: track x + 0.03}; it rolls at the release. Energy: a rolling ball needs a start about 2.7 × the loop radius above the loop's bottom to go round (height 0.45 m for a 15 cm loop just goes round; 0.35 m falls off). Goal loops {item, track}.
FALLING AND AIR: coffee-filters (count nested: terminal speed about 1 m/s × √count), parachute (canopy m across, load_mass kg: a bigger canopy, a slower fall), paper-sheet (falls slowly flat) vs paper-ball (the same 5 g crumpled, falls fast), feather. Drop them held at the same height (held: true, place {on: "air", y_m}) so they let go together. Vacuum or the Moon: scene settings {air: false} (and gravity "moon"): a feather and a hammer land together.
FORCE ARROWS AND ENERGY BARS (any moving item; from the run, so they are true to it): arrows ("all", "net", "all+net", or kinds joined by +: gravity, support (what it rests on pushing up), push (a wall, a paddle, a collision), friction, tension (ropes, cords, strings: each its own arrow when two or more pull it, a tug of war's two pulls), spring, air (resistance, or a fan's wind), buoyancy (water's and air's lift), magnetic, applied (a jet, a motor's push)); arrow_scale m of arrow per N (0 auto: the scene's biggest force about the thing's size). A free-body diagram of a book on the table: hardcover-book arrows "gravity+support" (equal and opposite: net 0); balanced and unbalanced pulls: a dynamics-cart between two pullers, arrows "tension+net" (or "all+net"); goal net_force {item, at_most_n?, at_least_n?} (with neither: its forces balance, net under 2 % of its weight). show_energy true draws small bars over the item; an energy-bars board (placed behind the scene, e.g. {on: "air", y_m: 1.0} beside the action, link watch = the moving thing; zero lowest (default) or floor) draws them large: kinetic, potential, spring, heat and sound; the total stays the start's. Goals energy_kept {item, tol?} (at most tol, 5 %, of the energy it had to spend turned to heat: a pendulum in a vacuum, settings {air: false}) and energy_to_heat {item, at_least_pct?} (10 %: a ball rolling to a stop on carpet, a bounce dying away).
ACTION AND REACTION, COLLISIONS: balloon-rocket (a balloon on a straw on a string `string` m long running from its anchor to the right, 1 m up: let go, it rushes forward; pressure Pa, nozzle m). clay-lump (sticks to the first moving thing it touches: drop it on a rolling cart to show momentum shared). Carts that collide: give one start_speed toward the other (velcro bumpers stick: they move on together at half the speed; magnet bumpers swap speeds).
  - goal balanced {item, part?, max_deg?, max_m?}: its main moving part (a lever's beam, a wheel and axle's wheel, a tackle's load, a pulled cart) moves less than max_m (1 cm) and turns less than max_deg (2°) all run: the forces or turning effects balance
  - goal loops {item, track}: the ball (or car) goes all the way round the coaster track's loop without falling off at the top
  - goal gear_speed {item, part?, rpm?, tol?, direction?}: its part (a gear train's last gear by default) turns, over the run's second half, at rpm (within tol, 10 %) and/or "clockwise" / "counter-clockwise"
  - goal rises {item, part?, min_m?}: its load (a wheel and axle's, a block and tackle's, a lever's, a screw jack's) ends at least min_m (5 cm; a screw jack's 1 cm) higher than it started
  - goal recoils {a, b, ratio?, tol?}: from rest (no start_speed on either), just after the push the two move off opposite ways (each at 2 cm/s or more); with ratio, a's speed ÷ b's just after the push is ratio within tol (10 %): equal and opposite pushes, speeds in the inverse ratio of the masses
  - goal pulls_with {item, newtons, tol?}: a force meter's steady reading (a puller's cord, an edge pulley's string: its newtons) is newtons within tol (5 %, at least 0.05 N): the median of its readings from 0.2 s after the release, slack moments left out (an inclined plane: m·g·sin θ while it pulls a cart up at a steady speed)
  - goal accelerates {item, accel, tol?}: from the release it speeds up at accel m/s² (within tol, 10 %) until it hits something or 1.5 s pass (F = ma: a hanging mass m on an edge pulley gives a cart M a = m·g/(M + m))
  - goal net_force {item, at_most_n?, at_least_n?}: the net force on it (the sum of every push and pull on it from outside: its force arrows' net, recorded in the run whether or not it shows arrows), the median from 0.1 s after the release, is at most at_most_n N and/or at least at_least_n N; with neither its forces balance (net under 2 % of its weight + 0.01 N): a book on a table, equal pulls on a cart, a parachute at its steady speed
  - goal energy_kept {item, tol?}: by the end at most tol (0.05 = 5 %) of the energy it had to spend (its start's kinetic, its potential above the lowest it went, spring energy, and anything put in) has turned to heat and sound: its energy only changed form (a pendulum or a ball on a smooth track with settings {air: false})
  - goal energy_to_heat {item, at_least_pct?}: by the end at least at_least_pct (10 %) of the energy it had to spend has turned to heat and sound (friction, bumps, the air): a ball rolling to a stop on carpet, a bounce dying away, a cart braking
  - knob lever-kit.effort: the effort's turning effect is its weight × its distance from the fulcrum; it balances when that equals the load's
  - knob lever-kit.effort_at: further from the fulcrum, the same effort turns the beam harder
  - knob lever-kit.load_at: a load nearer the fulcrum needs less effort to balance
  - knob wheel-and-axle.effort: effort × wheel radius against load × axle radius: more than the balance lifts the load
  - knob wheel-and-axle.wheel_radius: a bigger wheel round the same axle multiplies the effort more (MA = R/r)
  - knob block-and-tackle.effort: with n strands an effort of (load + block)/n holds the load; more lifts it
  - knob block-and-tackle.strands: each strand holding the moving block shares the load: n strands, 1/n of the effort
  - knob gear-train.rpm: every gear turns in proportion to the driver
  - knob gear-train.teeth_b: with two gears the second turns rpm × teeth_a ÷ teeth_b; more teeth, slower
  - knob gear-train.teeth_a: a driver with more teeth turns the others faster
  - knob coaster-track.height: a higher start gives the ball more energy: enough for the loop's top at about 2.7 × its radius above the bottom
  - knob coaster-track.size: a smaller loop needs less height to go round
  - knob ramp.blocks: a higher ramp gives what rolls down it more speed at the bottom
  - knob dynamics-cart.load: a heavier cart speeds up less under the same force (a = F/m) and carries more momentum at the same speed
  - knob dynamics-cart.plunger: a harder-cocked spring pushes the carts apart faster
  - knob edge-pulley.hanging_mass: a heavier hanging mass pulls the cart harder: a = m·g/(M + m)
  - knob puller.force: the bigger of two opposite pulls wins; equal pulls balance (net force 0)
  - knob pusher.force: a bigger push (force × time) gives more speed
  - knob balloon-rocket.pressure: more pressure, a stronger jet push
  - knob parachute.canopy: a bigger canopy has more air resistance: a slower fall
  - knob coffee-filters.count: more filters, the same shape: heavier for the same drag, they fall faster (about √n)
  - knob screw-jack.effort: the lifting force is efficiency × push × 2π × handle ÷ pitch
  - knob screw-jack.handle: a longer handle turns the screw with more force: the advantage is 2π × handle ÷ pitch
  - knob screw-jack.pitch: a finer thread lifts less a turn, so the same push lifts more weight (more slowly)
  - knob screw-jack.load: a lighter load needs less lifting force
  - knob screw-jack.turns: each turn lifts one pitch: faster turning, a faster lift (not a stronger one)
  - knob puller.speed: in speed mode it pulls at its set speed whatever force that takes (up to 100 N)
  - knob edge-pulley.drop: the hanging mass pulls only until it lands

  - knob cart.start_speed: a faster start carries it further (its kinetic energy, ½mv²)

### Light and optics
Light items shine in the scene's plane: a flashlight (a cone, lumens, beam_angle), a laser pointer (one thin beam), sunlight (parallel light at an elevation, in a band centred on its marker) and the heat module's desk lamp; a lit arrow is a lit object for lens images. Every optics item points where its `aim` prop says (degrees: 0 = right, 90 = up, 180 = left, -90 = down; leave the item's own angle at 0): a light shines along its aim; a mirror's shiny face, a light meter's sensor and an eye's look face along their aim (mirrors and meters default to 180, facing a light on their left); a lens's axis runs along its aim. Optics items stand on stands (they never fall): place them on "air" with y_m = the height of the beam (or on the table). Light goes straight until it meets something: opaque things (most items: balls, blocks, books, the table) stop it and cast shadows, mirrors reflect it (angle in = angle out; a mirror turned x° turns its beam 2x°; to send a beam arriving in direction A on in direction B, set the mirror's aim to (A + 180 + B) / 2), glass, water, ice and clear plastic bend it (a prism splits white light into a rainbow; a convex lens brings parallel light to a point focal_length behind it; a semicircular block totally reflects past 41°), material panels sort materials (transparent / translucent / opaque), colour filters pass their colour. Measuring: a light-meter reads lux on its sensor (sunlight ≈ 100 000 lx; a 150 lm flashlight at 1 m ≈ 1 600 lx in its beam; twice as far → a quarter), a light-sensor (target) registers whether a light reaches it, a screen shows shadows (its reading: the shadow's size; a point light makes the shadow grow as the object nears the light), an eye sees things that are lit (or lights) in front of it, also by mirrors. Light absorbed heats (each lit item's `light_w`). Liquids bend light too: the water (salt water, oil, syrup, honey, alcohol) in the liquids module's water-tank, beaker, graduated-cylinder, measuring-jug and density-column refracts with its own index (water 1.333, oil 1.47), its surface where the liquid stands now: a laser into an aquarium at 45° goes on at 32° in the water; a coin on the bottom of an opaque jug hidden behind its rim from an eye shows once there is water in it (sees {eye, coin}); a pencil standing in a beaker of water looks broken at the surface. The circuits module's bulbs and LEDs shine as lights too (as bright as their `light` reading: a bulb on 2 cells reads more lux on a light-meter than on 1; they cast shadows on a screen). A flashlight's `color` (white, red, green, blue) mixes on a white screen (red + green = yellow, all three white; two coloured torches make two coloured shadows); its `pattern` blinks a message (SOS in Morse code, or 1s and 0s, dot_s each) that a light-sensor or light-meter it reaches reads back: receives {sensor, light}.
  - goal hits_target {light, target, before_s?}: some of that light source's light reaches the target (straight, or by mirrors, lenses, glass)
  - goal lit {item, at_least_lux?}: at the run's end light falls on it (a light meter: it reads at least at_least_lux, default 1 lx)
  - goal dark {item, at_most_lux?}: at the run's end (almost) no light falls on it (a light meter: at most at_most_lux, default 1 lx)
  - goal shadow_on {occluder, screen}: the occluder's shadow falls on the screen (light that would reach the screen stops on it)
  - goal sees {eye, item}: light from the item (its own, or light it scatters) enters the eye, straight or by mirrors
  - goal brighter {a, b}: at the run's end light meter a reads more than b (other items: a takes in more light than b)
  - goal focused {screen}: a lit object's image on the screen is sharp (a convex lens between them at the right distances: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i)
  - goal receives {sensor, light, message?}: a blinking flashlight's message (its pattern: a Morse word such as SOS, or 1s and 0s) reaches the light-sensor or light-meter and reads back right (or reads `message`)
  - goal rainbow {screen}: white light split into its colours (a prism) lands on the screen, violet and red apart
  - knob flashlight.aim: points its beam (degrees: 0 right, 90 up)
  - knob flashlight.lumens: the light everywhere in its beam grows with its lumens
  - knob flashlight.beam_angle: a wider cone reaches more, each place dimmer
  - knob flashlight.dot_s: a longer dot sends the same message more slowly (the run must last the whole message)
  - knob measuring-jug.fill_ml: a higher water surface bends the light from what lies on the bottom further over the rim (the coin appears)
  - knob beaker.fill_ml: the water's surface is where light bends: more water covers more of what stands in it
  - knob laser-pointer.aim: points its beam (degrees)
  - knob laser-pointer.power_mw: more power, a brighter spot (same path)
  - knob mirror.aim: turning a mirror by x° turns its reflected beam by 2x°
  - knob curved-mirror.aim: points its face (and its focus)
  - knob curved-mirror.focal_length: its focus is focal_length in front of it
  - knob convex-lens.focal_length: parallel light meets focal_length behind it; an image forms where 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i
  - knob convex-lens.aim: its axis should run along the light
  - knob concave-lens.aim: its axis should run along the light
  - knob prism.aim: how the beam meets its faces sets how much it bends and spreads
  - knob glass-block.aim: a steeper slant bends the beam more
  - knob semicircle-block.aim: past the critical angle the light is totally reflected
  - knob light-meter.aim: a sensor facing the light reads the most
  - knob light-sensor.size: a bigger target catches more of a spread beam
  - knob screen.height: a taller screen catches more of the light and the whole shadow
  - knob eye.aim: it sees only what is in front of it
  - knob sunlight.elevation: a higher sun casts shorter shadows and puts more light on flat ground (∝ sin of its height)
  - knob sunlight.irradiance: how bright the sunlight is (clear noon ≈ 1000 W/m²)
  - knob lit-arrow.aim: points its light at the lens
  - e.g. "Show that light travels in straight lines": a laser-pointer (aim 0) and a light-sensor at the same height 1 m to its right (hits_target); a second laser with a cardboard material-panel between it and its own target: that target stays dark (dark {target})
  - e.g. "Make a shadow on a screen with a ball and a flashlight; nearer the light, a bigger shadow": flashlight aim 0 at y 0.3, a fixed tennis-ball 0.4 m to its right at the same height, a screen 1.2 m to its right (height 0.6): shadow_on {occluder: ball, screen}; its shadow_cm reading grows as the ball nears the light (5 cm card 20 cm from the light, screen at 60 cm: 15 cm)
  - e.g. "Bounce a laser off a mirror onto a target": laser-pointer aim 0; a mirror where the beam passes, aim (0 + 180 + 90)/2 = 135 to send it straight up; a light-sensor above the mirror: hits_target {light: laser, target}
  - e.g. "Show that light bends when it goes into glass (or water)": laser-pointer aimed down at aim -45 onto a glass-block on a stand; it bends to 28° inside and leaves parallel, shifted; a light-sensor on the exit path: hits_target
  - e.g. "Total internal reflection in a glass block": semicircle-block (aim 0: flat face right); a laser aimed through the round side at the middle of the flat face: 40° from the face's normal gets out, 43° is totally reflected back (a tir happening); light-sensors on both paths
  - e.g. "Which materials let light through? glass, wax paper, cardboard, foil": one lane each: flashlight (beam_angle 10) → material-panel → light-meter 5 cm behind it (aim 180); brighter {glass meter, wax meter}, lit {wax meter}, dark {cardboard meter}, dark {foil meter} (glass passes ≈ 92 %)
  - e.g. "A light meter near and far from a lamp: nearer is brighter": the desk lamp (aim 45, beam_angle 60, head_height 0.6) with two light-meters on its beam, 0.5 m and 1 m from the bulb, each aimed back at it: brighter {near, far} (about 4 : 1, 1/d²)
  - e.g. "We see a book because light bounces off it into our eye": a flashlight lighting a hardcover-book, an eye aimed at the book: sees {eye, book}; with the flashlight off (on false) the eye sees nothing (its sees reading 0)
  - e.g. "A convex lens makes an upside-down image": lit-arrow, a convex-lens (f 0.10) 0.30 m to its right, a screen 0.15 m behind the lens (1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i): focused {screen}; the screen's image_cm reading is −½ the arrow's height
  - e.g. "Split white light into a rainbow with a prism": sunlight through a slit (width 0.005) at elevation ≈ 24° from the left onto a flint prism turned apex down (aim 180), a screen beyond it: rainbow {screen}
  - e.g. "A magnifying glass focuses sunlight": sunlight at elevation 90, a convex-lens with aim 90 (axis vertical), a light-meter facing up (aim 90) focal_length below it: lit {meter, at_least_lux: 1000000}
  - e.g. "Black takes in more of the sun's light than white": sunlight on a white card and a black cloth material-panel lying flat (aim 90): brighter {black, white} (black absorbs ≈ 0.97, white ≈ 0.2)
  - e.g. "Colour filters: a red filter lets red light through and stops green": a flashlight (beam_angle 10) through a color-filter (color red) onto a screen, and a green laser-pointer through a second red color-filter onto a light-sensor: hits_target {torch, screen} (the red part passes, ≈ 0.88 of it), lit {sensor} labelled as a little green getting through (≈ 2 %)
  - e.g. "A lamp's light warms the ice cube it shines on": the heat module's lamp (target: the ice-cube it points at) and two ice-cubes on the table, one in its beam and one well away from it: hits_target {lamp, lit cube}, brighter {lit cube, other cube} (light taken in, W; with the heat module the lit cube melts first)
  - e.g. "See over a wall with a periscope": an eye low behind a wall (aim 180), a mirror in front of it at aim 45 and one above it at aim 225, a lit book on the far side above the wall: sees {eye, book}
  - e.g. "Light bends when it goes into water: a laser into an aquarium": a water-tank (aquarium, fill 0.2) on the table, a laser-pointer above its left half aimed down at aim -45 so the beam meets the water's surface: it goes on at 32° from the vertical in the water (n 1.333); a light-sensor on the tank's floor where the bent beam lands: hits_target {laser, sensor}
  - e.g. "The disappearing coin: a coin in a cup shows when water is poured in": a measuring-jug (opaque plastic) with a penny on its bottom, a flashlight above shining down into it, an eye beside it just below the rim's sight line looking at the bottom (aim about -60): with fill_ml 0 sees {eye, penny} fails, with fill_ml 500 it holds (the light from the coin bends over the rim)
  - e.g. "A pencil in a glass of water looks bent": a beaker of water with a chopstick or pencil leaning in it, lit by a flashlight, and an eye looking at it from the side and above: sees {eye, pencil}; the part under the water is seen at a steeper angle than the part above (the digest's beam path through the water shows the bend)
  - e.g. "Mix red, green and blue light; coloured shadows": three flashlights (color red, green, blue, beam_angle 30) a little apart aimed at one white screen, a ball between them and the screen: shadow_on {ball, screen}; where red and green overlap the screen looks yellow, all three white; the ball casts a coloured shadow for each torch
  - e.g. "Send a message with a flashlight (Morse code)": a flashlight with pattern SOS (dot_s 0.2, beam_angle 10) aimed at a light-sensor 1 m away, seconds 6: receives {sensor, light: flashlight} (it reads back SOS; the sensor's pulses reading counts the flashes)
  - e.g. "A bulb with 2 batteries is brighter than with 1": two circuits side by side (each a battery (1 or 2 cells) wired to a bulb), a light-meter 10 cm above each bulb facing down (aim -90): brighter {meter over the 2-cell bulb, meter over the 1-cell bulb}
### Soft and bendy things (elastic and plastic): squashing clay, bouncing and how high it bounces, bending rulers, stretched and wound rubber bands, coil springs
ELASTIC things squash, bend or stretch under a push and spring back (they store energy and give it back); PLASTIC things (soft-clay) squash and KEEP the dent. soft-clay: a modelling-clay ball (6 cm, 177 g): dropped or hit it flattens where it lands and stays flat, it barely bounces (dropped 1 m: a 7 mm flat); a heavy weight resting on it dents it a little; `softness` firm | normal | soft (warm clay dents deeper). Its force_n reads everything pressing on it (a 1 kg mass on it on the table: about 21 N, the mass's push and the table's). playground-ball (21.6 cm, 0.4 kg, `pressure` 14 kPa, at most 35), exercise-ball (65 cm, 1.1 kg, 4 kPa, at most 10) and foam-ball (7 cm squishy foam, `stiffness` kPa): they flatten where they land or are pressed and spring back round, bouncing. MORE AIR BOUNCES HIGHER: dropped 1 m (its bottom 1 m above the table) a playground ball's first bounce rises 0.27 m at 2 kPa (nearly flat), 0.41 m at 5, 0.55 m at 14, 0.61 m at 30 kPa; an exercise ball 0.20 m at 1 kPa, 0.39 m at 4, 0.46 m at 8. Less pressure (or softer foam) squashes more. Readings: squash_mm, force_n, energy_j (clay also dent_mm: the squash it keeps). Check a bounce with bounces {item, at_least_m?} or bounces_more {a, b}. Bending beams: flex-ruler is a ruler CLAMPED to a 10 × 5 cm wooden block that stands on the table; its anchor is the floor under the block's edge and its free part (`overhang`, default 0.2 m) sticks out to the right of x (`facing` left: to the left) at 5 cm + its thickness above the table. A load bends the end by F·a²·(3L − a)/(6EI) for a load centred a from the block's edge (at the very end, a = L: F·L³/(3EI)), so in a comparison put EVERY load's centre at the same distance from the block's edge: place {on: <ruler id>, x: <ruler x + overhang − (half the widest load's width + 0.01)>} on every ruler (gram-mass widths: 20 g 1.5 cm, 100 g 2.6 cm, 200 g 3.2 cm, 500 g 4.4 cm, 1 kg 5.5 cm; pennies, coin-flat, steel-washer, steel-weight-1kg too). Per 100 g at the end of 20 cm out: a wooden ruler (3.5 mm) about 2 mm, acrylic (3 mm) about 12 mm, aluminium (1.5 mm) about 4.5 mm, steel (0.5 mm) about 42 mm; twice the load twice the bend, twice the overhang 8 times. springboard (a diving board): a board bolted on a stand, its anchor the floor under the stand's edge, the board's top at stand_height + thickness. flex-plank: a plank, card strip or metal strip that rests on what is under it (anchor: the middle of its underside): lay it across two supports (two wooden-blocks or books, `fixed`, its ends resting on them) for a bridge that sags F·L³/(48·E·I) under a load in the middle. Wood and acrylic SNAP past their strength; steel, aluminium and card keep a permanent bend. Readings: bend_mm (the free end's drop, a plank's sag), energy_j, set_deg. band-launcher: a launch board (65 cm long, 12 mm thick: from 35 cm behind its anchor to 30 cm in front) with a rubber band between two posts at its anchor and the pouch (its tips 0.016·cos 25° in front of its back) pulled back `draw` m (default 0.1, at most 0.2: the band is then about 5 times its length; a rubber band SNAPS at 6 times, an event, and then throws nothing); put the thing to launch ON the board just in front of the pouch: place {on: <launcher id>, x: <launcher x − draw + half its length + 0.003>} (a toy-car's half length is 0.1 m; a ball's its radius) and set the band `height` above the board to the middle of the thing's back (a toy car 0.03, a ball its radius). At the release the band throws it forward (+x); tilt the launcher (angle_deg) to shoot up. Stored with 1 medium band: 0.13 J pulled 5 cm, 0.59 J at 10 cm, 1.5 J at 15 cm, 3.0 J at 20 cm (about as the square of the pull); each more band (`bands` 1-4) as much again; a thick `band` twice a medium one. A toy car on the board takes roughly half of it: pulled 15 cm it rolls about 3.8 m on a table, so give a launched car room or an end stop. Readings: stretch_cm, tension_n, energy_j, broken. Rubber-band cars: a toy-car, cart or truck with props {band_turns: 1-30} has a rubber band wound on its 3 mm rear axle that drives it forward when the scene lets go; `band_size` thin | medium (#64, default) | thick. On a table a toy car goes about: medium band 2 turns 0.4 m, 3 turns 0.9 m, 4 turns 1.5 m, 6 turns 3.1 m, 10 turns 7 m; thin band 5 turns 0.6 m, 10 turns 2 m, 15 turns 4 m, 20 turns 6.5 m; thick band 3 turns 1.8 m. So on a 3.7 m table compare few turns (2 vs 5 medium, or 5 vs 10 thin), or the car drives off its end. A band that pulls harder than the tyres grip SPINS THE WHEELS (an event) and the extra turns are wasted: a medium band past about 19 turns, a thick one past about 8; more turns never go less far. A 2 kg truck barely moves on one band. The distance comes from band_turns and band_size: never make a band car go farther with start_speed or a different surface under the other car. Readings: band_turns, band_stretch_cm, band_tension_n, band_energy_j. coil-spring: a coil spring on a base with a platform (anchor: the middle of the base's bottom; the platform's top about 2 cm + length above it): weights put on the platform (place {on: <spring id>}) squash it by weight ÷ stiffness (200 N/m: 4.9 mm per 100 g, 9.8 mm per 200 g: Hooke's law). Its readings are zeroed with its own platform resting on it, as a lab zeroes its scale: compression_mm (what the load squashes it), force_n (k × that: the load's weight), energy_j.
  - goal squashes {item, at_least_mm?}: it ends with a permanent dent at least that deep (default 1 mm): clay that keeps its squash
  - goal springs_back {item}: it squashes, bends or stretches at least 2 mm during the run and keeps no change of shape (no dent, no permanent bend, not snapped)
  - goal bends {item, at_least_mm?, at_most_mm?}: a ruler's, board's or plank's bend at the end (its free end's drop, a plank's sag) is within those mm (default at least 1); a bimetal-strip (the heat module's): its tip moves at least at_least_mm as it heats
  - goal deforms_more {a, b}: a ends more bent (or dented, or a spring more squashed; a ball's squash or a band's stretch at its most) than b, by 5 % and 0.2 mm or more (bends both under 1 mm: by a quarter and 0.02 mm; the result then says small)
  - goal stores {item, at_least_j?}: at its most it holds at least that much elastic energy (default 0.01 J): a stretched band, a bent board, a squashed spring or ball
  - goal bounces {item, at_least_m?, at_most_m?}: after its first landing it rises at least (at most) that high, its bottom over what it landed on (default at least 0.02 m): a dropped ball's first bounce
  - goal bounces_more {a, b}: a's first bounce rises higher than b's (by 5 % and 1 cm or more): a pumped-up ball against a flat one, dropped from the same height
  - knob flex-ruler.overhang: its bend grows as the overhang cubed: 26 % farther out bends it twice as much
  - knob flex-ruler.material: a stiffer material bends less: steel (E 200 GPa) and aluminium (69) at their usual thin gauges bend more than wood (12, 3.5 mm thick); acrylic (3.2) bends most of the thick ones (offered only for a ruler that is not compared with another: changing one of two would be a second difference)
  - knob flex-ruler.width: a wider ruler is stiffer: the bend falls as 1/width
  - knob springboard.length: the bend grows as the free length cubed
  - knob springboard.thickness_mm: the bend falls as the thickness cubed: a board twice as thick bends 8 times less
  - knob springboard.material: steel and aluminium are far stiffer than pine; acrylic and card far softer
  - knob flex-plank.length: a longer span sags more (∝ span³) — keep its ends on their supports
  - knob flex-plank.thickness_mm: the sag falls as the thickness cubed
  - knob flex-plank.width: the sag falls as 1/width
  - knob flex-plank.material: a stiffer material sags less (steel, aluminium, wood, pine, acrylic, card)
  - knob soft-clay.softness: soft clay flows at a lower pressure (0.08 MPa against 0.175 firm), so the same hit dents it deeper
  - knob soft-clay.diameter: a bigger ball is heavier (it lands harder) but spreads its flat wider
  - knob playground-ball.pressure: pumped harder it squashes less and bounces higher (dropped 1 m: 0.27 m at 2 kPa, 0.41 m at 5, 0.55 m at 14, 0.61 m at 30), levelling off past about 30 kPa (35 at most)
  - knob exercise-ball.pressure: pumped harder it squashes less under the same weight and bounces higher (dropped 1 m: 0.20 m at 1 kPa, 0.39 m at 4, 0.46 m at 8; 10 kPa at most)
  - knob foam-ball.stiffness: softer foam squashes more
  - knob band-launcher.draw: more stretch stores more energy (about as the square of the pull-back: 0.6 J at 10 cm, 3 J at 20 cm with one band), so it throws faster and farther; 20 cm at most (the band then 5 times its length: at 6 times it snaps)
  - knob band-launcher.bands: each more band pulls as hard again, storing more energy at the same pull-back
  - knob band-launcher.band: a wider band pulls harder (thin 1.6, medium 6.35, thick 12.7 mm wide)
  - knob coil-spring.stiffness: the squash is the weight divided by the stiffness
  - knob toy-car.band_turns: each turn winds 0.94 cm more band onto its 3 mm axle: more stored energy, a longer drive, until the band pulls harder than the tyres grip (a toy car: a medium band past about 19 turns, a thick one past about 8): then its wheels spin and the extra turns are wasted (offered only for a car that already has a band)
  - knob toy-car.band_size: a wider band stores more at the same turns (thick twice medium, medium 4 times thin) but spins the wheels sooner
  - knob cart.band_turns: each turn winds 0.94 cm more band onto its 3 mm axle: more stored energy, a longer drive, until the band pulls harder than the tyres grip (a toy car: a medium band past about 19 turns, a thick one past about 8): then its wheels spin and the extra turns are wasted (offered only for a car that already has a band)
  - knob cart.band_size: a wider band stores more at the same turns (thick twice medium, medium 4 times thin) but spins the wheels sooner
  - knob truck.band_turns: each turn winds 0.94 cm more band onto its 3 mm axle: more stored energy, a longer drive, until the band pulls harder than the tyres grip (a toy car: a medium band past about 19 turns, a thick one past about 8): then its wheels spin and the extra turns are wasted (offered only for a car that already has a band)
  - knob truck.band_size: a wider band stores more at the same turns (thick twice medium, medium 4 times thin) but spins the wheels sooner
  - e.g. "Does a ruler bend more with more coins on its end?": two flex-rulers (acrylic) at x 0.3 and 1.3, one with 2 pennies, one with 8 pennies on its end (place on the ruler at x + 0.185: the same distance from the block on both); goal deforms_more {a: ruler with 8, b: ruler with 2}
  - e.g. "Clay vs a bouncy ball dropped from 1 m": soft-clay and playground-ball held on air at y_m 1.0, 0.5 m apart; goals squashes {clay}, springs_back {ball}
  - e.g. "A ball pumped up with more air bounces higher": two playground-balls held on air at y_m 1.0, 0.6 m apart, pressure 20 and 3 kPa; goal bounces_more {a: the 20 kPa ball, b: the 3 kPa ball} (from 1 m about 0.59 m against 0.33 m)
  - e.g. "Pull a rubber band back farther to launch a car farther": two band-launchers (draw 0.05 and 0.15) in two lanes, a toy-car on each board in front of its pouch, room in front of each (the 15 cm one throws a car about 3.8 m on a table: an end stop or a long lane); goal farther {a: car of the 0.15 launcher, b: the other}
  - e.g. "Wind a rubber-band car more and it goes farther": two toy-cars in two lanes (one on a shelf plank above the other), props {band_turns: 5, band_size: thin} and {band_turns: 10, band_size: thin} (about 0.6 m and 2 m); goal farther {a: the 10-turn car, b: the 5-turn car}
  - e.g. "Hooke's law: hang more weight, more stretch": three coil-springs (200 N/m) 0.6 m apart with gram-masses 100 g, 200 g and 500 g on their platforms (place on: the spring); readings 4.9, 9.8 and 24.5 mm (zeroed with the platform on); goal deforms_more {a: the 500 g spring, b: the 200 g spring}
### Gravity and space (other worlds, orbits, the Moon's phases, eclipses, seasons, day and night on a globe)
PLACES (gravity of other worlds): the scene's settings say where it is. settings.gravity: "earth" (9.81 m/s², the standard), "moon" (1.62), "mars" (3.71), "jupiter" (24.79), "none" (0: weightless), or a number of m/s² for other worlds [NASA fact sheets]: Mercury 3.7, Venus 8.87, Saturn 10.44, Uranus 8.87, Neptune 11.15, Pluto 0.62. settings.air false = a vacuum (no drag, no buoyancy: a feather and a hammer fall together). settings.air_density (kg/m³, with air on; left out: a room's 1.2) is a world's own air for drag and buoyancy [NASA fact sheets]: Mars 0.020 (thin: a 1 g craft feather from 2 m lands 1.06 s after the drop, a golf ball 1.03 s; in a vacuum both 1.04 s), Venus 65 (thick: anything lighter than 65 kg/m³, a craft feather or foam, floats up), Jupiter 0.16, Saturn 0.19, Neptune 0.45 (their 1-bar levels). Real places: the Moon, Mercury, Pluto: air false; Mars {gravity: "mars", air_density: 0.02}; Venus {gravity: 8.87, air_density: 65}; Jupiter {gravity: "jupiter", air_density: 0.16}; a space station: gravity "none", air true; outer space: "none", false. (A module's own air processes, balloons and jars, use a room's air.) Same drop on different worlds: fall time √(2h/g) (1 m: Earth 0.452 s, Moon 1.111 s, Mars 0.734 s, Jupiter 0.284 s). Weight W = m·g changes with the place (a spring scale reads it), mass does not (a pan balance reads the same).
ORBIT MODE (sun, planet, moon, satellite): a scene with any of them is in space: NO uniform gravity and NO air, automatically (the machine plane is the plane of the orbits, seen from above). Bodies pull every moving thing with their real gravity at the scene's SCALE, which the heaviest body sets (its `scale`: auto = the Sun's "inner-planets" 1 m = 1 au, 1 s = 40 days; Earth's "earth-moon" 1 m = 300,000 km, 1 s = 2 days; Jupiter's "jupiter-moons" 1 m = 1 million km, 1 s = 12 h; Mars's "mars-moons" 1 m = 20,000 km, 1 s = 2 h; "low-orbit" 1 m = 10,000 km, 1 s = 10 min (the Earth drawn true size, 1.27 m across: satellites, Newton's cannon); "custom" km_per_m + hours_per_s). Real distances in scene metres = km ÷ km per metre: the Moon 384,400 km = 1.28 m (earth-moon); Mercury 0.387 m, Venus 0.723, Earth 1.0, Mars 1.524 (inner-planets); the ISS 6,791 km from Earth's centre = 0.679 m (low-orbit: only 4.2 cm above the 1.274 m Earth, so keep a satellite small there, size ≤ 0.05 m, or it grazes the ground); Io 0.422, Europa 0.671, Ganymede 1.070 (jupiter-moons). Newton's cannon: the Earth (low-orbit, fixed) with cannonballs (satellite kind cannonball, size 0.03-0.04) stacked straight above its top 6 cm apart, the lowest at 0.68 m from its centre: orbit_factor 0.7 falls back, 1.0 circles, 1.45 escapes.
Placing an orbit scene: the central body on "air" (place {on: "air", x, y_m}) at the middle, high enough that every orbit clears the table top (y = 0): centre y ≥ radius + 0.15 m; each orbiting body to its right at its distance (x = centre x + distance, same y), place on "air"; its `primary` link = the body it circles; orbit_factor 1 = a circle (counter-clockwise), 0.7 falls in, 1.2 an ellipse (it swings out to r·f²/(2 − f²)), 1.42 escapes. Set the stage (x0 x1 y0 y1) to hold every orbit with 0.2 m to spare, and seconds ≥ the periods you want to show (≤ 20). Real periods at the scale: Moon 13.7 s (earth-moon); Mercury 2.2 s, Venus 5.6 s, Earth 9.1 s, Mars 17.2 s (inner-planets); ISS 9.3 s (low-orbit); Io 3.5 s, Europa 7.1 s, Ganymede 14.3 s (jupiter-moons). MOON PHASES: the earth-moon scale (Earth at the middle, the Moon 1.28 m out, primary earth, orbit_factor 1) with a sun that only shines (props {pulls: false}) at one side of the stage: its light is parallel, as the real far Sun's, and the moon's phase as Earth sees it is read every moment (new when the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, full when Earth is between); never a pulling Sun near an Earth-Moon pair (the real Sun is 390 times farther away than the Moon: at a visible distance its pull tears them apart). The run shows the sidereal month (27.3 days), the phases in order. Sizes are automatic (true size at the scale, else a visible size, larger than true: say so); `fixed` holds a body still.
SHADOWS (gnomon, a shadow stick standing on the table or floor, its foot its anchor): latitude (Austin 30.27, + north), date (season: an equinox, a solstice, or day_of_year), solar time `hour` (12 = noon). The clock runs at the scene's settings.time_lapse: 3600 sweeps an hour a second (hour 8, seconds 8.5: 8:00 → 16:00). The shadow is drawn on the ground (the machine plane runs east-west: east to the right, north into the picture), shortest at solar noon pointing north (north of the tropics), toward the west in the morning and the east in the afternoon; the noon shadow is short in June, long in December (north). Readings: sun_elevation, sun_azimuth, shadow_m, shadow_dir, day_length_h; goal shadow_length {item, m, at_s?}. Austin, equinox: noon 0.58 m for a 1 m stick (Sun 59.7° up), 9:00 1.30 m; June solstice noon 0.12 m, December 1.36 m.
A geologist's hammer (rock-hammer, Apollo 15's 1.32 kg) for drop races: held (held: true) side by side with a feather, a ball or a paper at the same height, settings Moon + air false: they land together (goal lands_together).
CLASSROOM SUN-EARTH-MOON MODELS (globe, moon-ball: side view on the table, ordinary gravity; NOT orbit mode, so no sun item: a lamp plays the Sun). The light: the desk lamp (heat module) at one end of the table, head_height 0.4, target the globe (or a flashlight, or sunlight); a globe's or ball's lit_by link names it (none: the first light of the scene). globe = a 30 cm classroom globe on a stand, its foot on the table (y 0), its middle 0.40 m up (stand_height 0.25: level with the lamp's bulb), 0.8-1.5 m from the lamp: spin_rpm (6 = one turn, one day, every 10 s), tilt_deg 23.44, lean = where its north pole leans, kept so ("toward the camera" or "away from the camera" with the lamp to one side = an equinox; "toward the light" = the June solstice; "away from the light" = December's; right/left fixed in the room), start_hour (the town's solar time at the start: 6 sunrise, 12 noon, 18 sunset), town_lat (a red pin; Austin 30.27). The half facing the light is day; readings day (1/0), local_time, sun_elevation, noon_elevation, sun_lat (where the light is overhead), day_length_h, turns; events sunrise/sunset. Goals day_night {item: globe, is: "day"|"night", at_s?} or {item, days: n} (n sunrises and sunsets), noon_sun {item, deg, tol?}. Seasons on the table: one globe a run (a globe in line with another shades it: the readings do not see that shadow, the picture does), its middle level with the light: leaning toward the light = June (noon 83.2° at Austin, 13.9 h of day), away from it = December (36.3°, 10.1 h), to the side = an equinox (59.7°, 12.0 h); a light above the globe's middle raises where it is overhead (sunlight comes from 5° up at least). One run with the whole year: the Earth round the Sun in orbit mode with seasons on (below).
moon-ball = a white foam ball (Ø 7.5 cm) on a stick carried round a globe: its anchor is the circle's centre, so give it the globe's x and y (with around = the globe the centre IS the globe's middle); radius 0.6 m, period_s 12 (one trip = one month), start_deg 0 new moon (between the lamp and the globe), 90 first quarter, 180 full (behind the globe), 270 last quarter; it goes counter-clockwise seen from above (first quarter comes toward the camera when the lamp is on the left). tilt_deg 30 with node_deg 90 (the default) carries it above the globe's shadow at full and below the lamp's line at new: no eclipses; tilt_deg 0 (level) or node_deg 0: a lunar eclipse at full (the globe's shadow on the ball) and a solar one at new (the ball's shadow on the globe). Without a globe it goes round its own place (a viewer's eye: the head model). Readings elongation, lit, height, lunar_eclipse (0 none, 1 penumbral, 2 partial, 3 total), solar_eclipse (0, 1 partial, 2 annular, 3 total). Goals phase {item: the ball, name, any?, at_s?}, eclipse {type: "lunar"|"solar", item: the ball, total?, none?}.
ECLIPSES and SEASONS in orbit mode. The Moon's orbit is tilted 5.145° (moon orbit_tilt, automatic by body) and node_deg says where it crosses the Earth's orbit plane, from the Sun's direction at the start (default 90: high at full, low at new: NO eclipse this month, as most months; 0: the nodes line up with the Sun: a solar eclipse at the new moon and a lunar one at the full). Readings height_km, latitude (° above the plane), lunar_eclipse, solar_eclipse from the REAL sizes and distances (the bodies are drawn larger than true; the view lifts the Moon by the same factor so its drawn shadow matches). At the Moon's mean distance (the circle at 384,400 km) a central solar eclipse is annular: a total one needs it nearer (start it at perigee, 363,300 km = 1.211 m at the earth-moon scale, orbit_factor 1.027). Goals eclipse {type, item: the moon, total?, central? (solar: annular or total), none?, at_s?}, solar_eclipse {item, ...}, lunar_eclipse {item, ...}. SEASONS: a planet with seasons true (axis_tilt automatic: Earth 23.44), start_date (the date at the start: where its pole leans from the Sun), town_lat: its axis keeps pointing one way all round its orbit, so the Sun at noon climbs and sinks through the year: readings sun_lat, noon_elevation, day_length_h; goal noon_sun {item: the planet, deg, tol?, at_s?}; and night_lon, the midnight sky's ecliptic longitude (opposite the Sun: the stars change with the seasons): goal night_sky {item: the planet, constellation (the zodiac's 13 or Orion), at_s?, any?}: Orion high at midnight in December-January (night_lon 70-100°), Scorpius and Sagittarius in June-July. Sun at the middle (inner-planets: a year is 9.13 s), Earth 1 m out, start_date march equinox: noon at Austin 59.7° → 83.2° (June, a quarter year: 2.28 s) → 59.7° → 36.3° (December).

### Filming (fixed camera, starting gates)
Render only (the physics is untouched). settings.camera = {x0, x1, y, pitch?, hfov?} fixes the side camera: the machine plane spans x0…x1 m across the picture at height y m (the picture's centre line), looking down pitch° (default 6.843, the Wide shot's) through a lens of hfov° across (default 69.39, the Wide shot's 26 mm; 10-25 for a long track seen almost flat, so its metre marks are evenly spaced). Every run with the same camera is filmed from the same place: lanes run apart (one per run) line up pixel for pixel when stacked. Without it the Wide shot frames each run by itself (and never wider than x -1.5…4.5 m). start_gate: true on a HELD ball, toy vehicle or block (held: true, and the scene's release time) draws a starting gate instead of the pull pin: a dark bar on a post behind the track whose stop touches the item's front (its downhill side) and lifts away at the release; the item still starts exactly at rest at the release. turn_to_camera (degrees, 0-60) on a fan draws it turned toward the camera so its face and turning blades show (30 reads well); its air still blows the way it points.
### Sound and waves
Sound comes from something vibrating: a tuning-fork, plucked-ruler, drum, monochord (one guitar string), rubber-band (shoebox guitar), xylophone-bar, speaker, clapper or bell-jar sounds at its strike_at time (hits × every s apart), as loud as its strength (twice the strength = twice the vibration = 6 dB louder). Its PITCH is set by its own size and tightness: tuning-fork `pitch` (Hz); plucked-ruler `overhang` (shorter = higher, ∝ 1/overhang²; it clamps itself to the table's right edge, or its left edge with edge "left": two rulers = one on each edge); drum `tension` (∝ √tension) and `diameter`; monochord `length` (∝ 1/length), `tension` (∝ √tension), `gauge` (heavier = lower); rubber-band `width` (wider = lower), `length`, `tension`; xylophone-bar `length` (∝ 1/length²); glass-bottle `fill` (tapped: more water = lower; blown: more water = higher). A sound-meter is the LISTENER (no people): it reads dB (A-weighted by default) where its microphone is; sound falls 6 dB per doubling of distance, arrives after distance ÷ 343 m/s, reflects off Wall items (an echo: the meter's `echo` reading is the delay) and is soaked up by a sound-panel (foam, curtain). In a vacuum (scene settings.air false) nothing travels through the air; the bell-jar shows that by pumping its own jar empty. A meter set to listen "touching" and pressed against a steel-rod, wooden-rod, plank or the table also hears what that solid carries (faster than air: steel 5050 m/s); a hydrophone's probe hung under the water of a water-tank (Liquids) hears a source in that water at 1481 m/s. An oscilloscope's microphone (on a little stand 21 cm to its right, or left with mic_side) listens like a meter and its screen draws the wave it hears: louder = taller waves (amplitude: `scale` Pa a square), higher = more waves across its 10 squares (pitch × 10 × `time_base`: 440 Hz at 1 ms a square shows 4.4 waves). Rice grains laid ON a drum's head jump when it is struck (harder = higher). A ball that hits a drum, fork or xylophone bar sounds it. Sound lines and audio in the video are automatic. Waves: a wave-rope (v = √(tension ÷ weight per metre)) or slinky (push and pull = compressions like sound; v = L·√(k/m)) is shaken at its left end by a driver (one pulse or keep shaking at `frequency`); its far end is tied (a pulse comes back upside down), a ring on a pole (same way up) or runs on (nothing comes back): use those two on a rope lying "on the floor" (held up, a free end hangs μgL²/(2T) down onto the table); a ribbon on it only moves across (the wave carries energy, not the rope); driven at f = n·v/(2L) a tied rope shows n standing loops (goal standing {item, loops}): give it a SMALL shake (amplitude ≤ 0.02 m), damping ≥ 1 (the default 1.5 is a real rope's) and ≥ 4 s, and the picture settles within a few seconds; a big shake or damping 0 makes loops that never settle. A rope is cut into segments of ≤ 2.5 cm and ≥ 10 a wavelength (up to 800): waves shorter than about 4 segments do not travel (a warning says so). A held-up rope or Slinky lies on the table where it would sag or swing below it. Rice on a drum (or a ball on a fork) is thrown only by the drum's own strikes (strike_at, hits), never by landing on it; strike it AFTER the scene's release (release + 0.3 s): the head rings only ≈ 0.2 s, so a strike before the grains are let go throws them little. Every drum hit moves its head at the same speed for the same strength (loose or tight: rice jumps alike); harder (strength) throws higher (× strength²); a heavy thing on a drum barely moves. A ripple-tank's dipper makes water waves (wavelength from frequency, depth and the scene's gravity); its duck or cork bobs in place (goal stays_put); a ripple tank always stays level. Goals for waves: wave_reaches, reflects, standing, wavelength {item, m}, wave_speed {item, m_s}, stays_put; for an oscilloscope's picture: trace {oscilloscope, waves_across, squares_high}. Pendulum timing: a pendulum's period is 2π√(L/g) (the `period` goal measures it). A string-telephone is two paper cups with a string between their bottoms, held level (no stand: place it on: air, y_m 0.2-0.5 over the table; its anchor is the string's middle, so its cups reach length/2 + 0.09 m either side: give the stage room). Its own child talks into its LEFT cup (voice: whisper by default, quiet, normal, loud, shout, or none for a speaker or fork put at that cup; talk_at, talk_for). Pulled taut (pull 2-10 N, 5 by default) the string carries the sound to its RIGHT cup: about 24 dB under what goes into the left cup for 3 m of cotton string (3 dB more a metre; steel wire about 16 dB; fishing line 29 but only 0.5 dB more a metre). The ear is a sound-meter with its microphone at the right cup's mouth: meter x = phone.x + length/2 + 0.12, its height = the phone's height over what the meter stands on (within 50 cm of a cup's mouth it hears the string; the voice goes either way). A whisper reaches it through the string (about 39 dB(A)) but not through the air (about 30 dB 3 m away, under a quiet room's 35). Slack (pull 0), drooping (under about 0.2 N) or pinched (pinched true) it carries nothing or little: only the air is left. Its readings: carries (0/1), loss_db, sag_mm, string_ms (≈ 1600 m/s along cotton: faster than the air). Goals: hears {meter, source: the telephone} and, for a slack or pinched one, hears {meter, source, expect: false}.
  - goal sounds {source, pitch_hz?, tol_hz?, at_least_db?}: the source (a tuning fork, drum, ruler, string, bar, speaker, clapper, bell, buzzer) makes a sound during the run, at that pitch (within tol_hz, default 2 %), at least that loud 1 m away
  - goal higher {a, b}: a's note is higher (a higher pitch, more vibrations a second) than b's; both must sound
  - goal louder {a, b, at?}: a is louder than b (two sound meters: their loudest readings; two sources: their level 1 m away, or with at = a sound meter, how loud each is there)
  - goal hears {meter, source, at_least_db?, expect?}: the sound meter hears the source (its sound reaches the meter at least as loud as the quiet room, or at least at_least_db); expect false: it does not (a slack or pinched string-telephone)
  - goal echo {meter, delay_s?, tol?}: the sound meter hears an echo off a wall (delay_s after the first sound, within tol: default 5 ms; delay = extra path ÷ 343 m/s)
  - goal wave_reaches {item, x?, before_s?}: the wave on a wave rope or Slinky (or a ripple tank's ripples) reaches its far end, or x m along it, by before_s if given
  - goal reflects {item, way?}: a pulse on a wave rope or Slinky comes back from its far end, way "upside down" (a tied end), "same way up" (a ring on a pole) or "none" (it must not come back: the rope runs on)
  - goal jumps {item, min_m?}: something of the item (rice grains on a drum's head, a ball by a tuning fork) is thrown up at least min_m (default 5 mm) above where it started
  - goal standing {item, loops?}: a wave rope or Slinky kept shaking shows a standing wave of `loops` loops at the end (a tied line driven at f = n·v/(2L) shows n; give it damping ≥ 1 and a small shake, ≤ 2 cm, and at least 4 s)
  - goal wavelength {item, m?, tol?}: the waves on a wave rope, Slinky or ripple tank are m metres long (speed ÷ frequency; within tol m, default 5 %)
  - goal wave_speed {item, m_s?, tol?}: the waves on a wave rope (√(T/μ)), Slinky (L·√(k/m)) or ripple tank run at m_s m/s (within tol, default 5 %)
  - goal stays_put {item, max_drift_m?, min_bob_mm?}: what rides the waves bobs but goes nowhere: a ripple-tank's duck or cork bobs ≥ min_bob_mm (default 0.5) while drifting ≤ max_drift_m (default 1 cm); a wave rope's or Slinky's ribbon moves ≥ min_bob_mm and travels no more than max_drift_m along (waves carry energy, not the water or rope)
  - goal trace {oscilloscope, waves_across?, squares_high?, tol?}: an oscilloscope's screen at its loudest shows that many waves across (pitch × 10 × time a square) and that many squares high (its pressure ÷ Pa a square), each within tol × it (default 0.1 = 10 %); without numbers, that it shows a wave
  - goal period {item, seconds?, tol?}: the item (a pendulum, a rope pendulum, a swing, a weight on a hanging spring) swings back and forth, once every `seconds` (within tol, default 2 %), measured from the run (frequency = 1 ÷ period)
  - knob plucked-ruler.overhang: the ruler's pitch goes as 1 ÷ overhang²: 15 cm → 35 Hz, 10 cm → 79 Hz
  - knob monochord.length: a string's pitch goes as 1 ÷ its length: half as long is an octave higher
  - knob monochord.tension: pitch goes as √tension: four times the tension is an octave higher
  - knob rubber-band.tension: pitch goes as √tension
  - knob rubber-band.width: a wider band is heavier per length: lower pitch
  - knob xylophone-bar.length: a bar's pitch goes as 1 ÷ length²
  - knob drum.tension: a drum's pitch goes as √(head tension)
  - knob tuning-fork.pitch: the fork's pitch is its own (a shorter-pronged fork is higher)
  - knob drum.strength: twice the strength is twice the head's speed: +6 dB, and grains thrown off 2× faster (4× higher); a loose or a tight head throws them alike
  - knob tuning-fork.strength: twice the strength: +6 dB
  - knob plucked-ruler.strength: twice the strength: +6 dB
  - knob speaker.level: its level 1 m away, in dB
  - knob tuning-fork.strike_at: when it sounds
  - knob drum.strike_at: when it sounds; rice on it jumps only when it is struck after the scene lets things go (the head rings ≈ 0.2 s)
  - knob sound-meter.room: what it reads with nothing sounding
  - knob wave-rope.tension: v = √(tension ÷ weight per metre)
  - knob wave-rope.frequency: wavelength = speed ÷ frequency; a tied rope shows n loops at f = n·v/(2L)
  - knob wave-rope.amplitude: how far the driver moves the rope's end; a standing wave needs ≤ 2 cm to settle into clean loops
  - knob wave-rope.damping: how fast its motion dies away (1/s): a standing wave settles in about 3 ÷ damping seconds
  - knob wave-rope.length: a longer rope: the wave takes longer to cross; a tied rope's loops at f = n·v/(2L)
  - knob slinky.amplitude: how far the driver moves its end
  - knob wave-rope.far_end: tied: a pulse returns upside down; ring on a pole: the same way up; runs on: no reflection
  - knob slinky.stiffness: v = L·√(k/m)
  - knob slinky.frequency: wavelength = speed ÷ frequency
  - knob ripple-tank.frequency: faster dipping: shorter water waves (v = f·λ)
  - knob ripple-tank.depth: shallow water waves run at about √(g·depth)
  - knob ripple-tank.amplitude: how far the dipper bobs: the duck bobs that much where it floats
  - knob oscilloscope.scale: a smaller Pa a square draws the same sound taller
  - knob oscilloscope.time_base: a longer time a square shows more waves across
  - knob glass-bottle.fill: tapped, more water lowers the note; blown, more water (less air) raises it
  - knob bell-jar.air_left: the bell's sound reaching the room falls with the air in the jar
  - knob string-telephone.pull: a taut string carries the voice (2-10 N); under about 0.2 N it droops and carries little, at 0 nothing
  - knob string-telephone.pinched: a pinched string cannot vibrate past the fingers: nothing gets through
  - knob string-telephone.voice: a louder voice into the near cup is louder at the far one, and through the air too
  - knob string-telephone.length: cotton string loses about 3 dB a metre (fishing line 0.5, wire almost none)
  - e.g. "A shorter ruler makes a higher sound": two plucked-ruler items on the table's right edge (one per table or one at a time), overhang 0.15 and 0.10 (35 → 79 Hz); goal higher {a: the 10 cm one, b: the 15 cm one}
  - e.g. "Hit the drum harder and the rice jumps higher and it is louder": two drums (strength 0.5 and 1.0, or hits at different times), rice ON each head (rice y = drum height), struck 0.3 s or more after the release, a sound-meter between them; goals jumps {item: rice}, louder {a: harder drum, b: softer drum}
  - e.g. "The farther away, the quieter the tuning fork sounds": a tuning-fork and sound-meters 1, 2 and 4 m away (microphones at the fork's height); each doubling reads 6 dB less; goals hears {meter, source} and louder {a: near meter, b: far meter}
  - e.g. "An echo off a wall 17 m away comes back a tenth of a second later": a wide stage (x to 20 m), a clapper and a sound-meter just behind it, a Wall 17.15 m away (height 3); goal echo {meter, delay_s: 0.1}
  - e.g. "A guitar string an octave higher when it is half as long": two monochords: length 0.648 and 0.324 (329.6 → 659 Hz); goal higher {a: short, b: long}
  - e.g. "A pulse on a rope reflects upside down from the tied end": a wave-rope (length 4, tension 10 N, weight 0.1 kg/m: 10 m/s), shake one pulse, far_end tied to the post; goals wave_reaches {item: rope, before_s: 1}, reflects {item: rope, way: "upside down"}
  - e.g. "A standing wave with 3 loops on a rope": a wave-rope length 4, tension 10, weight 0.1 (v 10 m/s), keep shaking at f = 3·10/(2·4) = 3.75 Hz, amplitude 0.015, damping 1.5, seconds 6; goal standing {item: rope, loops: 3}
  - e.g. "A duck bobs on ripples but stays where it is": a ripple-tank (depth 0.02, frequency 5, floater duck at 0.6), seconds 4; goal stays_put {item: tank} (readings floater_bob_mm and floater_drift ≈ 0)
  - e.g. "Faster dipping makes shorter water waves": two ripple-tanks, frequency 5 and 10 Hz; goals wavelength {item: each, m: its wavelength reading} (v = f·λ)
  - e.g. "A ball hitting a xylophone bar makes it ring": a xylophone-bar with a ball held above it (or rolling off a ramp onto it); goal sounds {source: bar}
  - e.g. "A bell in a jar goes quiet as the air is pumped out": a bell-jar (pump_at 1, pump_for 4, air_left 0) and a sound-meter 1 m away; the meter's level falls by about 35 dB
  - e.g. "Shorter xylophone bars ring higher": xylophone-bars 0.20 and 0.141 m long (779 → 1558 Hz); goal higher
  - e.g. "A pendulum's swing time depends on its length": pendulums of different length; goal period {item, seconds} (T = 2π√(L/g): 1 m → 2.0 s)
  - e.g. "A bottle xylophone: more water, lower note": four glass-bottles (fill 0.1, 0.35, 0.6, 0.85, play tap) tapped one after another (strike_at 0.4, 0.9, 1.4, 1.9); goals higher {a: emptier, b: fuller}
  - e.g. "On an oscilloscope, a louder sound makes taller waves and a higher sound makes the waves closer together": two speakers far apart (3 m: 440 Hz at 70 dB and 880 Hz at 70 dB, or the same pitch at 60 and 72 dB), an oscilloscope with its microphone 30 cm from each (time_base 1 ms a square: 4.4 and 8.8 waves across); goals hears {meter: scope, source: its speaker}, louder {a: the louder speaker's scope, b: the other}
  - e.g. "A string telephone carries a whisper when the string is pulled tight, and nothing when it is slack": two string-telephones of 3 m cotton string, one above the other (y_m 0.3 and 0.9 over the table, x 1.3), each with its own child whispering; the top one pull 5 N (taut), the bottom one pull 0 (slack); a sound-meter at each right cup (x 2.97, height 0.3 on the table; the top one on: air with height 0.12 at y_m 0.78); goals hears {meter: top meter, source: taut phone}, hears {meter: bottom meter, source: slack phone, expect: false}
  - e.g. "Sound travels faster through water than through air": a water-tank (Liquids), a tuning-fork (box false) standing in its water, a hydrophone beside the tank with its probe under the water (reach over the wall), a sound-meter in the air; the hydrophone's at:fork reading is distance ÷ 1481 m/s
### Scene settings (plan.settings; an edit: set_scene {settings})
settings: {gravity: "earth" | "moon" | "mars" | "jupiter" | "none" or m/s² 0…30, air: true | false (false = a vacuum: no drag, no buoyancy, fans move nothing), air_density: kg/m³ 0.001…100 with air on (a world's own air for drag and buoyancy: Mars 0.020, Venus 65, Jupiter 0.16; left out: a room's 1.2), room_temp: °C −60…60 (where heat starts and cools to), time_lapse: 1…100000 (seconds of slow processes, heating, melting, cooling, per second of the run; motion stays real-time)}. Leave it out for an ordinary room.

# The catalog: the ONLY things that can be in a scene
Every item has: id, type (one of the keys below), props (only the keys listed for its type, inside their ranges; leave a prop out to keep its default), held, fixed.
Units: metres, kilograms, seconds, degrees (counter-clockwise), m/s. "*x*" marks a choice's default; "=v" a prop's default; "[a…b]" its allowed range.
Outline = the item's box at its default props and angle 0, relative to its anchor (x right, y up): use it to know how tall/wide a thing is and where its bottom is (an item resting on a surface at height h has its anchor at y = h − outline.y0 … i.e. h + |y0|).
Static = fixed in place (it never moves; it can be placed in mid-air, but must visibly stand on or hang from something: its legs, its cords, or a support item). Dynamic = falls and moves (set "fixed": true to pin it, "held": true to hold it until the scene's release time).
How the view draws what holds things up: a held item rests on a small wooden pull pin on a thin wooden post behind the machine until the release (so in a picture, a thin post or pin holding a ball or weight at its top IS that held state: build the thing with held true; the post is neither an item nor missing); a fixed top point or pivot (a pendulum's or a wrecking ball's hanger) stands on its own retort stand (a steel rod on a heavy foot, with an arm) or a wall bracket, which is part of that item; a plank stands on wooden legs while its legs prop is on. "Looks:" says each type's colour and kind, where it matters for matching a picture.
Every type also has the surface props material, bounce 0…1, friction 0…2, rolling 0…0.5, side 0…1, even where its list below leaves them out. Where two things touch, the engine uses the measured value for their two materials when it has one, scaled by how far each item's own friction is from its material's: pair friction = measured × √(fa/fa₀ × fb/fb₀) (no measured pair: √(fa × fb)); so halving ONE item's friction lowers the pair's by only about 30 %: quarter it, or halve both, to halve the pair. Bounce: measured × (ba/ba₀)(bb/bb₀), else ba × bb. A thing on a slope slides when tan(angle) > the pair's friction; the run's events, not the props, say what really happened. (material: a choice, its default shown; rolling = rolling resistance; side = the sideways spring-back of grippy balls.) Change them only when the request asks for a surface behaviour, or to make a run work without changing how a thing looks.
