Notes: also called: paper towel, filter paper, wick, capillary action, chromatography, walking water, paper strip, absorb.

mod_fracture.title: Breaking things and padding (eggs, glass, plates, windows, bridges, glued towers)
mod_fracture.text:
### Breaking things and padding (eggs, glass, plates, windows, bridges, glued towers)
Things that BREAK when a force passes a real threshold: raw-egg (cracks at 35 N: about a 5 cm drop onto a hard floor; smashes into shell pieces and a spill when hit twice as hard), drinking-glass (shatters: about a 46 cm drop onto a hard floor), ceramic-plate (breaks into sherds: about 35 cm), window-pane (window glass, mount frame = fixed upright in a wooden frame, or loose: a baseball moving faster than about 4 m/s shatters a 3 mm pane, a gentle toss bounces off; thicker glass or a soft ball takes more), snap-bridge (a beam of spaghetti, craft sticks, chalk or a chocolate bar across two supports, with its supports: put loads ON it at its x and it bends and snaps; strands = how many pieces of made_of lie side by side, so strands 1 is one chocolate bar or one stick of chalk: set it from the request whenever you change made_of; 5 spaghetti strands over a 20 cm gap hold about 175 g pressed at one point in its middle, and a wide load spreads its bending and holds more: a 3.5 cm steel weight about 15 % more; more strands or a shorter gap hold more), block-tower (wooden blocks, loose or glued: a hard knock makes loose blocks fall off and tape let go, white glue hardly ever; it reads blocks_fallen and top_height, and a block that only slides along still stands). For any egg that should crack or break use raw-egg (it cracks at 35 N, about a 5 cm drop onto a hard floor, and breaks into pieces); the mechanics module's egg {fragile: true} is a simpler egg with no pieces (it cracks from about 7 cm): use it only when the plain egg is asked for. PADDING saves them: a cushion (material foam, packing foam, bubble wrap, cotton balls, pillow stuffing, crumpled paper, folded towel, carpet; thickness) under where it lands, or any pillow, foam block, sponge, carpet strip or rubber mat; other modules' soft things cushion by their own squash too: an inflated playground or exercise ball, a foam ball, a clay ball, a trampoline's mat (an egg dropped 50 cm onto an exercise ball or 1 m onto a trampoline survives). Thicker and softer padding saves it from higher (an egg: 5 cm of soft foam from about 50 cm, a pillow from about 95 cm). Hard on hard (a glass dropped on a glass, a rim on a rim) breaks at half the force of a flat landing. WATER: a breakable dropped into a water-tank's water is slowed by it and only its hit on the tank's floor counts, so an egg dropped 30 cm into 20 cm of water survives where one dropped onto the table smashes; a raw egg sinks in fresh water and floats in salt water of 12 % or more (the fluids module's floats / sinks goals). The tank's liquid is the water: never stand a cushion in for water. TABLES AND SHELVES: for "falls off a table" or "knocked off a shelf", stand it on the real table or on a shelf that stands on something (a plank on two wooden blocks or posts; never a plank hanging in the air), or hold it (held: true, on air at y_m) at that height and say so. The egg-drop challenge is ONE item, egg-drop-box (padding, padding_thickness, parachute = canopy width in m: 0.4-0.8 slows a box to 2-4 m/s; a parachute does nothing in a vacuum or a pumped vacuum jar): drop it held: true at a height (place on air with y_m). To load an egg (books or a weight resting on it) make it fixed: true (held in a carton: a loose egg rolls out from under a load); it cracks under a resting 35 N (3.6 kg). Each breakable reports broken (0 whole, 1 cracked, 2 in pieces), peak_force (N), share (peak over its breaking force) and impact_speed; a bridge also load (N) and sag. Goals: breaks {item, before_s?}, survives {item}, breaks_first {item, other}, knocked_down {item, at_least_blocks?}.
  - goal breaks {item, before_s?}: a breakable item (raw-egg, drinking-glass, ceramic-plate, window-pane, egg-drop-box's egg, snap-bridge, block-tower: a glued joint lets go or a block falls off; any item with a broken reading) cracks, shatters, snaps or comes apart (by before_s if given)
  - goal survives {item}: a breakable item never breaks in the run (an egg that is padded well enough, a bridge that holds its load)
  - goal breaks_first {item, other}: item breaks, and before other does (or other never breaks)
  - goal knocked_down {item, at_least_blocks?}: a block-tower is knocked down: half its blocks or more fell, or it stands less than half as tall as it was built; with at_least_blocks, that many of its blocks fell (a block that only slides along still stands)
  - knob cushion.thickness: thicker padding squashes farther, so what lands on it stops more gently and feels less force
  - knob cushion.material: softer padding (pillow stuffing, foam, cotton) gives a smaller force than stiff packing foam or carpet; too thin a soft pad squashes flat and stops it hard
  - knob egg-drop-box.padding_thickness: more padding round the egg stops it more gently (up to what the box has room for)
  - knob egg-drop-box.padding: soft padding (cotton balls, pillow stuffing, foam) protects the egg; stiff packing foam much less
  - knob egg-drop-box.parachute: a bigger canopy slows the fall, so the box lands slower (in air only: nothing in a vacuum)
  - knob egg-drop-box.size: a bigger box has room for more padding round the egg
  - knob snap-bridge.strands: each strand carries its own share of the bending: twice the strands hold twice the load
  - knob snap-bridge.span: the bending a load makes grows with the gap: half the gap holds about twice the load in the middle
  - knob snap-bridge.made_of: craft sticks are far stronger than spaghetti, chalk and chocolate far weaker (strands keeps its count: that many of the new pieces)
  - knob block-tower.glue: loose blocks fall off when hit; tape lets go under a hard knock; white glue hardly ever
  - knob window-pane.thickness: thicker glass is stiffer and much stronger (its breaking force grows with its thickness squared): a 6 mm pane takes about 4 times the force of a 3 mm one
  - knob raw-egg.strength: hen eggs break at 30-40 N; outside that it is no longer a real egg
  - knob drinking-glass.strength: a tempered glass is about 4 times as strong as an annealed one
  - knob ceramic-plate.strength: porcelain and stoneware vary about twofold in strength
  - e.g. "Drop three raw eggs from 50 cm: onto the table, onto a foam pad and onto a pillow. Which survive?": three raw-egg held: true on air at y_m 0.5 above their landing, side by side 40 cm apart: one over the bare table, one over a cushion {material: foam, thickness: 0.05}, one over a cushion {material: pillow stuffing, thickness: 0.15}; goals breaks {the egg over the table}, survives {each padded egg}
  - e.g. "How many strands of spaghetti hold 300 g across a 25 cm gap?": snap-bridge {made_of: spaghetti, span: 0.25, strands: 6} and another {strands: 12} side by side, a steel-weight-1kg {mass: 0.3} placed on each bridge at its middle; goals breaks {the 6-strand bridge}, survives {the 12-strand bridge} (10 strands hold about 320 g of a 3.5 cm weight)
  - e.g. "Egg-drop challenge: a padded box with a parachute against a bare box, from 1.5 m": egg-drop-box {padding: cotton balls, padding_thickness: 0.03, parachute: 0.6} and egg-drop-box {padding: none, parachute: 0}, both held: true on air at y_m 1.5, side by side; goals survives {the padded box}, breaks {the bare box}
  - e.g. "Does a glass break if it falls on the floor? What about on a carpet?": two drinking-glass held: true on air at y_m 0.6, one over the bare table, one over a cushion {material: carpet, thickness: 0.01}; goals breaks {the glass over the table}, survives {the glass over the carpet}
  - e.g. "Knock down a loose tower and a glued tower with a rolling ball": block-tower {glue: none} and block-tower {glue: white glue} 1.2 m apart, each with its own plank ramp (angle -30) and a bowling-ball held at its top; goals knocked_down {the loose tower}, survives {the glued tower}
  - e.g. "Throw a baseball at a window": a window-pane {mount: frame} standing on the table, a baseball 1 m to its left given start_speed 9 (m/s) toward it (start_dir 0); goal breaks {the pane}; a second pane with the ball at start_speed 2 survives
  - e.g. "Drop an egg into a tank of water and another onto the table from 30 cm": a water-tank {fill: 0.2} and a raw-egg held: true 30 cm above its water; a second raw-egg held 30 cm above the bare table; goals survives {the egg over the water}, breaks {the egg over the table}
### raw-egg — Raw egg · dynamic
A raw hen's egg that breaks: it cracks when a force on it passes its breaking force (35 N: dropped about 5 cm onto a hard floor) and smashes into shell pieces and a spill when hit twice as hard. Padding under it (a cushion, a pillow) lets it fall much farther. Facts: 57 g · cracks at 35 N (a 5 cm drop on a hard floor).
Anchor (x, y): its centre. Outline at defaults: 0.062 × 0.048 m, centred on the anchor.
Props: length: m =0.057 [0.03…0.1]; width: m =0.044 [0.02…0.08]; mass: kg =0.057 [0.01…0.3] auto (follows length, width unless set); strength: N =35 [5…200].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): broken (Broken: 0 whole, 1 cracked, 2 in pieces), peak_force (Biggest force, N), share (Of its breaking force, ×), impact_speed (Hardest hit, m/s).
Notes: also called: egg, raw egg, fragile, breakable, egg drop, crack, shell.
### drinking-glass — Drinking glass · dynamic
An annealed glass tumbler that shatters into shards when an impact's force passes its breaking force: dropped bottom-first onto a hard floor from above about 46 cm; a carpet or a cushion saves it from higher. Facts: 250 g · shatters from about a 46 cm drop onto a hard floor.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its bottom. Outline at defaults: 0.075 × 0.1 m; from the anchor x −0.037…+0.037, y +0…+0.1.
Props: diameter: m =0.075 [0.04…0.15]; height: m =0.1 [0.05…0.25]; mass: kg =0.25 [0.02…2] auto (follows diameter, height unless set); strength: N =1840 [100…20000].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): broken (Broken: 0 whole, 1 cracked, 2 in pieces), peak_force (Biggest force, N), share (Of its breaking force, ×), impact_speed (Hardest hit, m/s).
Notes: also called: glass, tumbler, cup, fragile, breakable, shatter, glassware.
### ceramic-plate — Ceramic plate · dynamic
A stoneware dinner plate that breaks into four sherds when an impact's force passes its breaking force: dropped flat onto a hard floor from above about 35 cm. Facts: 450 g · breaks from about a 35 cm drop onto a hard floor.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its bottom. Outline at defaults: 0.26 × 0.025 m; from the anchor x −0.13…+0.13, y +0…+0.025.
Props: diameter: m =0.26 [0.1…0.4]; height: m =0.025 [0.01…0.06]; mass: kg =0.45 [0.05…3] auto (follows diameter unless set); strength: N =2470 [100…20000].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): broken (Broken: 0 whole, 1 cracked, 2 in pieces), peak_force (Biggest force, N), share (Of its breaking force, ×), impact_speed (Hardest hit, m/s).
Notes: also called: plate, dish, dinner plate, ceramic, porcelain, fragile, breakable.
### cushion — Cushion pad · dynamic
A pad of padding: foam, packing foam, bubble wrap, cotton balls, pillow stuffing, crumpled paper, a folded towel or carpet. A breakable thing that lands on it squashes it and feels a much smaller force than on a hard floor; thicker and softer padding saves it from higher. (Any pillow, foam block, sponge, carpet or rubber mat pads the same way.) Facts: 30 × 30 cm · 5 cm of soft foam. Moving parts ≈135 g.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its bottom. Outline at defaults: 0.3 × 0.05 m; from the anchor x −0.15…+0.15, y +0…+0.05.
Props: width: m =0.3 [0.03…2]; thickness: m =0.05 [0.005…0.5]; depth: m =0.3 [0.03…2].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): squash (Squashed, m).
Surface: material *foam* | packing foam | bubble wrap | cotton balls | pillow stuffing | crumpled paper | folded towel | carpet; bounce 0.15, friction 0.7, rolling 0.06, side 0.
Notes: also called: cushion, padding, pad, foam, pillow, bubble wrap, cotton, landing pad, soft, mat.
### egg-drop-box — Egg-drop box · dynamic
The egg-drop challenge: a raw egg inside a cardboard box, padded all round, with a parachute if you like. When the box lands, the egg is pressed by its padding (softer and thicker padding: less force) or only by its share of the box's slowing on a soft landing; it cracks at 35 N. A parachute slows the fall. Facts: 15 cm box · cotton balls 3 cm thick. Moving parts ≈175 g.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its bottom. Outline at defaults: 0.15 × 0.15 m; from the anchor x −0.075…+0.075, y +0…+0.15.
Props: size: m =0.15 [0.08…0.4]; padding: none | foam | bubble wrap | *cotton balls* | crumpled paper | pillow stuffing | packing foam; padding_thickness: m =0.03 [0…0.15]; parachute: m =0 [0…1.5]; strength: N =35 [5…200].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): broken (Broken: 0 whole, 1 cracked, 2 in pieces), peak_force (Biggest force, N), share (Of its breaking force, ×), impact_speed (Hardest hit, m/s).
Notes: also called: egg drop, egg drop challenge, capsule, container, padding, parachute, box, engineering, design.
### snap-bridge — Snapping bridge · dynamic, on a fixed frame or pivot (it does not fall)
A beam of spaghetti, craft sticks, chalk or a chocolate bar across the gap between two supports. Put weights on it: it bends, and snaps where the bending passes its strength (5 strands of spaghetti over a 20 cm gap hold about 175 g in the middle). More strands hold more; a wider gap holds less. Facts: 5 strands of spaghetti over a 20 cm gap. Moving parts ≈10.4 g.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of the floor under the gap. Outline at defaults: 0.3 × 0.103 m; from the anchor x −0.15…+0.15, y +0…+0.103.
Props: made_of: *spaghetti* | craft sticks | chalk | chocolate bar; strands: int =5 [1…60]; span: m =0.2 [0.03…0.6]; support_height: m =0.1 [0.02…0.5].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): broken (Broken: 0 whole, 1 cracked, 2 snapped), load (Load on it, N), share (Of its strength, ×), sag (Sag, m).
Notes: also called: bridge, spaghetti bridge, beam, snap, break, load, strength, chalk, craft sticks, popsicle sticks.
### block-tower — Block tower · dynamic
A tower of wooden blocks stacked one on another, loose or held together with sticky tack, tape, a glue stick or white glue. Loose blocks fall off when hit hard (a block that only slides along still stands); glued ones move as one until a joint's strength is passed (white glue: hardly ever). It reports how many blocks fell and how tall it stands now. Facts: 6 wooden blocks, 10 × 5 × 5 cm. Moving parts ≈1.05 kg.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base. Outline at defaults: 0.1 × 0.305 m; from the anchor x −0.05…+0.05, y +0.001…+0.306.
Props: blocks: int =6 [1…20]; block_width: m =0.1 [0.02…0.4]; block_height: m =0.05 [0.01…0.3]; block_depth: m =0.05 [0.01…0.3]; glue: *none* | sticky tack | tape | glue stick | white glue.
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): broken (Came apart: 0 no, 1 yes), blocks_fallen (Blocks fallen), top_height (Height now, m), share (Of the glue's strength, ×).
Notes: also called: tower, blocks, stack, glued, tape, structure, knock down, engineering.
### window-pane — Window pane · static (fixed in place)
A pane of window glass (3 mm) in a wooden frame, or loose. A ball thrown hard at it shatters it into shards that fall; a gentle toss bounces off. Thicker glass, or a smaller pane, takes a harder hit; a soft ball (a playground ball) hits it more gently than a hard one (a baseball). Facts: 60 × 60 cm · 3 mm glass · shatters at 258 N (a baseball at about 4 m/s).
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its bottom. Outline at defaults: 0.06 × 0.68 m; from the anchor x −0.03…+0.03, y +0…+0.68.
Props: height: m =0.6 [0.1…1.5]; width: m =0.6 [0.1…1.5]; thickness: m =0.003 [0.002…0.012]; mount: *frame* | loose; strength: N =258 [20…20000] auto (follows height, width, thickness unless set).
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): broken (Broken: 0 whole, 1 cracked, 2 in pieces), peak_force (Biggest force, N), share (Of its breaking force, ×), impact_speed (Hardest hit, m/s).
Surface: material glass; bounce 0.92, friction 0.4, rolling 0.001, side 0.1.
Notes: also called: window, window pane, pane, glass sheet, sheet of glass, glass, broken window, fragile, breakable, shatter.

mod_granular.title: Sand, gravel and soil: piles, craters, pouring, sand timers, erosion
mod_granular.text:
### Sand, gravel and soil: piles, craters, pouring, sand timers, erosion
Granular items are FIXED in place (static) and stand on what is under them (the table, a ramp, a tray): sand-pile (a heap of `sand_kg` kg at its angle of repose, or shape "castle": a packed tower `width` × `height`), sand-tray (a wooden box filled level with `sand_depth` of grains: drop balls into it for craters, roll things into it), sand-funnel (a funnel of `sand_kg` kg on a ring stand, its spout `height` m over its base; at the release it pours at Beverloo's steady rate and heaps up below), hourglass (a sand timer: `sand_kg` kg through a `neck_mm` neck; 66 g of fine sand through 3 mm = 60 s; its top bulb holds about 0.75·bulb_cm³ g of fine sand: 5 cm 94 g, 6 cm 160 g, 8 cm 380 g) and stream-table (a tray tipped `tilt_deg`, damp sand over `sand_share` of it from the high end, a hose of `flow_lpm` at the high end from the release, a pool `lake_cm` deep at the low end). Anchors: a pile's at the middle of its base on the surface; a funnel's under its spout, on the surface its stand stands on (the stand's foot is drawn beside the heap, about 6 cm past the funnel's rim); a tray's and an hourglass's at the middle of their base; a stream table's at the middle of its tipped floor. A heap must fit on what it stands on: a plank or a shelf is only 12 cm deep, so a heap wider than it (over about 300 g of sand) runs off its edge before the run, falls to what is below and reads spilled_g (the run says "<heap> does not fit on <plank>"); for a big heap use the table or a sand-tray (grains rest only on FIXED things: never on a ball, a car or a board that can move). Grains (`grain`): sand 0.4 mm (dry repose 34°), fine sand 0.18 mm (32°), coarse sand 1 mm (35°), gravel 6 mm (38°), pebbles 2 cm (40°), soil (35°, sticky), flour (45°: the crater medium); the kitchen's: sugar 0.5 mm (35°, 800 kg/m³ poured: 200 mL is 160 g), salt 0.4 mm (32°, 1200 kg/m³), rice (long grains, 32°, 770 kg/m³; a spout or neck must be over 14 mm for it). `wetness`: dry (flows, heaps at its angle of repose), damp (sticks: a castle up to about 23 cm stands with straight walls; taller, it crushes and slumps), soaked (slumps to 20-28°). A dry castle collapses into a cone in a fraction of a second; a damp one stands. Pouring: a funnel's flow is Beverloo's W = 0.58·ρ_b·√g·(D − 1.4d)^2.5: sand through a 10 mm spout 25 g/s, 20 mm 140 g/s. A spout or neck jams (clogs) under about 5 grains: dry fine sand needs over 0.9 mm, sand 2 mm, coarse sand 5 mm, gravel 30 mm, pebbles 10 cm; flour arches over anything under 20 mm and soil under 15 mm; damp sand jams in any funnel. A heap's height grows with the cube root of its mass; its slope stays the angle of repose. Poured heaps: to show the heap a funnel pours, use the funnel ALONE: never put a sand-pile under a funnel (a ready-made cone is not what was poured). The funnel itself reads its heap (heap_mm, heap_deg, heap_g), and piles {item: the funnel}, steeper {a: funnel, b: funnel} judge that poured heap. Which grains heap steepest: one funnel per grain side by side (about 0.6 m apart), each with a spout wide enough for its grains (sand 10-15 mm, gravel 40 mm, flour 25 mm), sand_kg 0.2-0.3, and seconds enough for each to empty. Sand timers: an hourglass runs only dry fine sand (neck over 0.9 mm), sand (over 2 mm) or coarse sand (over 5 mm); gravel, pebbles, soil and flour jam in any neck it has (12 mm at most). A jammed timer reads clogged 1 ("jammed"), its clock (run_s) stops and the run says "<timer> jams: its grains arch over the 3 mm neck": widen the neck past 5 grains or use finer grains. The hourglass is its own clock: time it by its run_s and the timer goal (lesson seconds, with the scene's time-lapse); a stopwatch can time it too: watch = the hourglass, stop = reads (stop_reading empty, stop_value 1: it stops as the sand runs out), counts lesson under a time-lapse (its face then shows lesson seconds, and a reads goal's seconds are those). Craters: hold a ball above a sand-tray (place it in the air over the tray, held, released at the scene's release): it strikes, throws sand out and is buried; the crater follows Uehara et al.'s law, D ≈ 0.9·(ρ_ball/ρ_sand)^¼·D_ball^¾·H^¼/√(tan repose): a 2.5 cm steel ball from 0.6 m about 9 cm, from 1 m about 10 cm; a ping-pong ball only about its own size (4-4.5 cm), whatever the height: a heavier ball, or a higher drop, makes a wider crater. In sand thinner than the ball goes (a 1 cm layer), it hits the floor and the crater is smaller. Compare two trays side by side. A ball or a toy car rolled into sand ploughs and stops. Erosion: a stream-table needs time: set the scene's settings.time_lapse (10-30) so seconds of the run are minutes of the lesson (the sand changes that much faster; the water runs as it does). More slope, more water or finer grains erode more; gravel hardly moves; plants ("lower half", "all") protect the sand they cover. Two tables side by side differing in ONE prop make a fair test. Readings each run: a pile's height_mm, width_mm, angle_deg, mass_g (on what it stands on), spilled_g; a tray's crater_mm (rim to rim), crater_depth_mm; a funnel's left_g, poured_g, flow_gs, clogged, heap_mm, heap_deg, heap_g (the heap it poured); an hourglass's top_g, bottom_g, flow_gs, run_s (lesson seconds), empty, clogged; a stream table's eroded_g (sand carried off the slope), delta_cm, channel_mm. Containers keep grains: a glass-jar (made wider and lower it is a dish, narrower and taller a glass; set its depth to its width), cup, plastic-cup, bucket, basket, box, beaker, graduated-cylinder, measuring-jug, coffee-mug or bowl that grains pour into (from a funnel, or a pitcher of grains: the flow module's pitcher with contents "grains") or that a sand-pile is laid in (its anchor on the container's floor) holds every grain inside its round or square walls: they pile up in it at their angle of repose, a bed that fills it topped by a cone once the heap reaches its wall (400 g of sand in a 6.5 cm glass: a 10.5 cm bed and cone, nothing outside). The pourer's heap_mm, heap_deg and heap_g are read inside the container; outside_g is what missed it (a pile's spilled_g). A funnel's spout or a cup's lip goes over the opening's middle (grains fall nearly straight down). A kitchen-scale weighs the grains resting on its platform or in a bowl or coffee-mug standing on it (a heap poured on it from a funnel above it, a sand-pile set on it: on: the scale, or sugar poured into a bowl on it: the bowl and the sugar); a fixed cup, jar, beaker, bucket or box holds its own grains (a scale under one weighs neither): measure's reads {item: scale, grams}; its tare zeroes a heap set on it before the release. Known limits: sieving (separating sand from gravel or pebbles by grain size) is the matter module's mixture-dish and sieve, not these items.
  - goal piles {item: sand-pile, or sand-funnel for the heap it pours, min_deg?, max_deg?}: at the end it stands as a heap at least 5 mm tall, its slope (angle_deg, a funnel's heap_deg) within the bounds
  - goal stands {item}: a sand-pile (a castle) ends at least 90 % as tall as it started
  - goal collapses {item}: a sand-pile (a castle) ends under 70 % of the height it started at
  - goal steeper {a, b}: heap a's slope ends at least 1° steeper than heap b's (sand-piles, or sand-funnels for the heaps they pour)
  - goal crater {item: sand-tray, min_mm?}: a crater at least min_mm (default 10) wide rim to rim ends in the tray
  - goal crater_bigger {a, b}: the crater in sand-tray a ends clearly wider than the one in tray b (by 2 mm and 5 %)
  - goal sand_runs_out {item: sand-funnel or hourglass, before_s?, after_s?}: its grains all run out (within those run seconds); for liquids use the flow module's empties
  - goal runs_out_first {a, b}: funnel/hourglass a runs out of sand clearly before b (by 2 % of b's time), or b never does
  - goal timer {item: hourglass, seconds, tol_s?}: it runs out after `seconds` lesson seconds, within tol_s SECONDS (default 5 % of seconds; an old `tol` under 1 is read as a share: 0.1 = 10 %); run_s counts the scene's time-lapse, and stops while a jam blocks the neck
  - goal clogs {item: sand-funnel or hourglass}: its grains jam in the spout or the neck (too narrow for them)
  - goal erodes {item: stream-table, min_g?}: the water carries at least min_g (default 20) g of sand away from where it lay
  - goal erodes_more {a, b}: the water erodes clearly more sand in stream table a than in b (by 10 g and 5 %)
  - goal delta {item: stream-table, min_cm?}: the sand the water drops reaches at least min_cm (default 1) past the sand's toe toward the pool
  - knob sand-funnel.outlet_mm: a wider spout pours faster (Beverloo: as the width to the 2.5) and stops jamming once it is over about 5 grains wide (gravel needs 3-4 cm, flour 2-3 cm)
  - knob sand-funnel.sand_kg: more grains make a bigger heap (its height grows as the cube root of its mass) and take longer to pour
  - knob sand-funnel.grain: finer dry grains pour through a narrower spout; gravel jams in small spouts, flour arches over them; a steeper heap needs coarser or stickier grains (gravel 38°, flour 45°)
  - knob hourglass.sand_kg: the time is the sand's mass over the steady flow: twice the sand runs twice as long (a jammed neck never runs, whatever the sand)
  - knob hourglass.neck_mm: the flow grows as the neck's width to the 2.5: a neck a quarter wider runs out in about 0.6 of the time; a neck under 5 grains wide jams (coarse sand needs over 5 mm, sand 2 mm, fine sand 0.9 mm): widening it past that is the honest fix when the grains are the person's choice
  - knob hourglass.neck_mm: with a timer goal: a neck widened past 5 grains (the jam's honest fix when the grains are the person's) with the sand that keeps the goal's time (sand = seconds × the flow; a bigger bulb when the top one cannot hold it)
  - knob hourglass.grain: finer grains pass a narrower neck (it must be over 5 grains wide) and run a little faster; gravel, pebbles, soil and flour jam in any timer's neck
  - knob sand-pile.sand_kg: a bigger heap is taller and wider at the same slope (on a 12 cm plank, over about 300 g of sand spills off)
  - knob sand-pile.wetness: damp sand sticks (a castle stands); dry sand slumps to its angle of repose; soaked sand slumps flatter
  - knob sand-pile.height: a damp sand castle taller than about 23 cm crushes under its own weight (coarse sand about 9 cm)
  - knob sand-tray.sand_depth: a crater needs sand deeper than the ball goes (a few cm); too shallow and the ball hits the floor and the crater is smaller
  - knob sand-tray.grain: flour and fine sand show crisp craters; gravel barely dents
  - knob stream-table.tilt_deg: a steeper slope makes the water faster and its push on the sand stronger: more erosion
  - knob stream-table.flow_lpm: more water flows deeper and faster: it carries more sand
  - knob stream-table.grain: fine sand and soil wash away easily; coarse sand less; gravel hardly moves
  - knob stream-table.plants: roots and stems hold the sand they cover: the water cannot pick it up there
  - knob stream-table.sand_depth: deeper sand lets the channel cut deeper before it reaches the tray
  - e.g. "Pour sand from a funnel onto the table to see it make a cone-shaped pile.": a sand-funnel (sand_kg 0.3, outlet_mm 10, height 0.25) on the table, nothing under it; seconds ≥ mass ÷ 25 g/s + 2; goals sand_runs_out {funnel}, piles {funnel} (its poured heap)
  - e.g. "Pour sugar into a glass jar and see it pile up.": a glass-jar on the table and a sand-funnel of sugar (grain sugar, sand_kg 0.15, outlet_mm 12, height 0.25) at the jar's x, its spout over the jar's middle; seconds ≥ 150 g ÷ 20 g/s + 2; the jar keeps every grain; goal piles {funnel} (its heap in the jar)
  - e.g. "Pour dry sand from one funnel and gravel from another: which makes the steeper pile?": two sand-funnels side by side (sand: outlet_mm 12; gravel: outlet_mm 40), sand_kg 0.25 each, NO sand-pile under them; goal steeper {a: gravel funnel, b: sand funnel} on their poured heaps
  - e.g. "Drop a steel ball into sand from a low and a high height: which makes the bigger crater?": two sand-trays side by side, a steel-ball held over each (place on air, x = the tray's x, y_m 0.6 and 0.2); goal crater_bigger {a: high tray, b: low tray}
  - e.g. "Make a sand timer that runs out in about 30 seconds.": an hourglass of fine sand (sand_kg 0.033 with the 3 mm neck: 1.1 g/s), settings.time_lapse 4 and seconds 12; goal timer {item, seconds: 30} (5 % by default; tol_s is in seconds)
  - e.g. "Build a sandcastle from damp sand and one from dry sand: which stands?": two sand-piles with shape castle, wetness damp and dry; goals stands {damp}, collapses {dry}
  - e.g. "Does a steeper stream table erode more sand? (5 minutes)": two stream-tables (tilt_deg 12 and 4), settings.time_lapse 20, seconds 15; goal erodes_more {a: steep, b: gentle}
### sand-pile — Sand pile · static (fixed in place)
A heap of sand, gravel, soil, flour, sugar, salt or rice on whatever it rests on, or a packed sandcastle. Dry grains stand at their angle of repose (sand 34°, gravel 38°, flour 45°, sugar 35°, salt and rice 32°) and slide down when piled steeper; damp sand sticks and stands in walls; soaked sand slumps. Balls and blocks sink into it and are slowed by it. A heap wider than the shelf or plank it is on spills off its edge. Facts: 1 kg of dry sand: a cone about 13 cm wide, 4.5 cm tall at 34°.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base, on what it rests on. Outline at defaults: 0.192 × 0.065 m; from the anchor x −0.096…+0.096, y +0…+0.065.
Props: shape: *heap* | castle; sand_kg: kg =1 [0.01…20]; width: m =0.08 [0.02…0.5]; height: m =0.12 [0.01…0.6]; grain: *sand* | fine sand | coarse sand | gravel | pebbles | soil | flour | sugar | salt | rice; wetness: *dry* | damp | soaked; sand_color: *natural* | red | blue | green | yellow | purple | white | black | pink | orange.
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): height_mm (Height, mm), width_mm (Width, mm), angle_deg (Slope, °), mass_g (Mass, g), spilled_g (Spilled, g).
Notes: also called: sand, pile, heap, mound, sandcastle, castle, gravel, soil, dirt, flour.
### sand-tray — Sand tray · static (fixed in place)
A wooden tray filled level with sand, flour or soil. Drop a ball into it: it makes a crater (bigger from higher, and for heavier balls) and is buried; roll something into it: it ploughs in and stops. Facts: 50 × 35 cm, 5 cm of sand: about 14 kg.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its floor's underside, where it stands. Outline at defaults: 0.524 × 0.092 m; from the anchor x −0.262…+0.262, y +0…+0.092.
Props: length: m =0.5 [0.15…3]; width: m =0.35 [0.1…1]; wall: m =0.08 [0.02…0.3]; sand_depth: m =0.05 [0.005…0.3]; grain: *sand* | fine sand | coarse sand | gravel | pebbles | soil | flour | sugar | salt | rice; wetness: *dry* | damp | soaked; sand_color: *natural* | red | blue | green | yellow | purple | white | black | pink | orange.
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): crater_mm (Crater, mm), crater_depth_mm (Crater depth, mm), sand_mm (Sand depth, mm).
Notes: container, but NOT usable as a goal container; also called: sandbox, sand pit, crater, impact, meteor, flour, long jump, tray, box of sand, moon craters.
### sand-funnel — Funnel of sand · static (fixed in place)
A funnel of grains on a ring stand. At the release its spout opens and the grains pour out at a steady rate (Beverloo: it does not slow as the funnel empties) and heap up below at their angle of repose. Too narrow a spout for the grains (gravel, or sticky flour or damp sand) and it clogs. Over a jar, glass, cup, bowl or box the grains stay inside it and heap up within its walls. Facts: 1 cm spout: about 25 g of sand a second.
Anchor (x, y): under its spout, on what its stand's foot stands on (the foot is beside the heap). Outline at defaults: 0.25 × 0.295 m; from the anchor x −0.19…+0.06, y +0…+0.295.
Props: sand_kg: kg =0.3 [0…5]; outlet_mm: mm =10 [2…60]; funnel_cm: cm =12 [5…40]; height: m =0.2 [0.03…1.5]; delay: s =0 [0…20]; grain: *sand* | fine sand | coarse sand | gravel | pebbles | soil | flour | sugar | salt | rice; wetness: *dry* | damp | soaked; sand_color: *natural* | red | blue | green | yellow | purple | white | black | pink | orange.
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): left_g (Left, g), poured_g (Poured, g), flow_gs (Flow, g/s), clogged (Clogged: 0 no, 1 yes), heap_mm (Heap height, mm), heap_deg (Heap slope, °), heap_g (Heap, g), outside_g (Outside, g).
Notes: acts at the scene's release time; also called: funnel, pour, pouring, sand, pile, heap, angle of repose, clog, jam, flow rate.
### hourglass — Hourglass (sand timer) · static (fixed in place)
A sand timer: grains run from the top bulb through the neck at a steady rate (whatever the height of sand above) and heap up in the bottom bulb. It reads how long it has run (lesson seconds, with the scene's time-lapse). A neck narrower than about 5 grains jams: nothing runs and its clock stops. Facts: 66 g, 3 mm neck: 60 s.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base. Outline at defaults: 0.08 × 0.134 m; from the anchor x −0.04…+0.04, y +0…+0.134.
Props: sand_kg: kg =0.066 [0.001…2]; neck_mm: mm =3 [0.8…12]; bulb_cm: cm =5 [2…15]; grain: sand | *fine sand* | coarse sand | gravel | pebbles | soil | flour | sugar | salt | rice; delay: s =0 [0…20]; sand_color: *natural* | red | blue | green | yellow | purple | white | black | pink | orange.
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): top_g (Top, g), bottom_g (Bottom, g), flow_gs (Flow, g/s), run_s (Ran, s), empty (Empty: 0 no, 1 yes), clogged (Jammed: 0 no, 1 yes).
Notes: also called: hourglass, sand timer, egg timer, timer, clock, time, minute, measure time.
### stream-table — Stream table · static (fixed in place)
A tipped tray of damp sand with a hose at its high end and a pool at its low end. The water carves a channel down the slope, carries the sand and drops it where it slows in the pool: a delta. Steeper, more water or finer grains: more erosion; gravel and plant roots resist it. Set the scene's time-lapse (e.g. 15) to see minutes in seconds. Facts: 1 L/min on 6°: a channel and a delta in about 5 minutes.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its tray's floor. Outline at defaults: 0.908 × 0.214 m; from the anchor x −0.454…+0.454, y −0.057…+0.157.
Props: tilt_deg: ° =6 [0…25]; flow_lpm: L/min =1 [0…6]; sand_depth: m =0.05 [0.01…0.12]; sand_share: =0.6 [0.2…0.9]; lake_cm: cm =2 [0…6]; plants: *none* | lower half | upper half | all; length: m =0.9 [0.4…2.5]; width: m =0.4 [0.15…1]; grain: *sand* | fine sand | coarse sand | gravel | pebbles | soil | flour | rice; wetness: dry | *damp* | soaked.
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): eroded_g (Eroded, g), delta_cm (Delta, cm), channel_mm (Channel, mm), water_lpm (Water, L/min).
Notes: also called: stream table, erosion, deposition, river, delta, weathering, landform, water, sand, canyon.

mod_hands.title: Hands (a person holds, lets go, pushes, pours)
mod_hands.text:
### Hands (a person holds, lets go, pushes, pours)
Render only (the physics is untouched): a person's hand where a person acts, real size, the arm running out of the picture. props.hand on a HELD thing (held: true; it lets go at the scene's release): auto | pinch | palm | press | grip — a hand holds it instead of the pull pin; at the release the fingers open and the hand moves out of the picture (a thing with start_speed is thrown: the hand follows through first). auto picks: a fingertip pressing a floater down in water (press), thumb and finger round a small thing (pinch), the open palm under a ball or block in the air (palm), the whole hand from above round a thing that rests on something (grip). props.hand_from: auto | left | right | above (where the arm comes from). On a FIXED thing (fixed: true) props.hand holds it the whole run instead of its stand (a magnet held in a fist: grip). A pusher's props.hand: finger | hand | two hands | fist draws the push as a person's at the paddle's face (its housing, rod and paddle not drawn); the push's strength is its force and push_time, never the hand: a harder push is more force, and the skin says only finger, hand or two hands. A pitcher's props.hand: hand — a hand holds it by its handle (a cup round its body) and tips it.

mod_heat.title: Heat and temperature: melting ice and salt, lamps, hot plates, thermometers, insulation, boiling and evaporation
mod_heat.text:
### Heat and temperature: melting ice and salt, lamps, hot plates, thermometers, insulation, boiling and evaporation
Heat runs in a scene that holds a heat item (salt-pile, plate, bowl, lamp, thermometer, hot-plate, saucepan, drink-cup, spoon, meltable, puddle) or sets settings.room_temp or settings.time_lapse; then every moving thing has a temperature: ice cubes (ice-cube, start_temp_c −18 °C from a freezer) melt and shrink, their melt water runs into a puddle; steel-rod (material copper, aluminium, steel, stainless steel or glass) and wooden-rod conduct along their length; a fluids container's water (water-tank, beaker, measuring-jug, graduated-cylinder) has the temperature of its water_temp_c, and its level (level_mm) follows heat's water: floating ice that melts leaves the level where it was, evaporation lowers it. The room is settings.room_temp (default 20 °C; a classroom 22). TIME-LAPSE: melting, cooling and evaporating take minutes to hours, so set settings.time_lapse (lesson seconds per run second) so that seconds × time_lapse covers the story; motion stays real-time. A 2.5 cm ice cube melts in about 50-60 min on a ceramic plate at 22 °C, a 4 cm cube in about 1 h 40 min, a 5 cm cube in about 2 h 30 min (from −18 °C a little longer); 1 L of water on a 600 W hot plate boils in about 15 min; a hot drink cools 80 → 50 °C in 20-60 min; a puddle (1.5 mm deep, whatever its size) dries in about 12 h at 22 °C, sooner under a lamp. E.g. seconds 12 with time_lapse 600 shows 2 hours. Goal times are minutes of LESSON time, the clock on screen (by_min, at_min: 2 h = 120), never run seconds. Ice and salt: put the ice cube ON a plate or IN a bowl (place {on: <plate id>} / {inside: <bowl id>, on: <bowl id>}), centred; a salt-pile goes ON the ice cube (place {on: <cube id>}): it dissolves into the melt water and makes salt water that melts ice below 0 °C, so the salted cube melts sooner (1 g on a 4-5 cm cube: a few % sooner; 6 g: 10-30 % sooner; in a bowl the brine stays longer). A bigger cube takes far longer (a 5 cm cube ≈ 3 × a 2.5 cm one), so a big salted cube still loses to a small plain one. What the cube stands on matters: aluminium plate ≫ ceramic > glass or plastic (melamine) > foam. Lamps: a lamp (desk lamp, static) shines a cone of light and heat: set props.target to the item it should heat (it then aims at it) and put the lamp 15-30 cm to one side of it (x), head_height 0.25-0.45 m. Its heat on a target falls as 1/distance² (60 W incandescent: about 240 W/m² at 25 cm, 600 at 15 cm; sunlight 1000): a lamp on one of two cubes makes it melt sooner (10-25 %). An LED bulb (bulb led) gives light but almost no heat. Only what its beam reaches warms; something in between shades it. Measuring: a thermometer reads what its bulb (its anchor, the bottom end) is in or touches, else the air; it lags (glass: 8 s in water, 60 s in air; digital: 3 s / 30 s) and reads high in a lamp's beam. To read a cup's water put it in the cup ({inside: <cup id>, on: <cup id>}) with fixed true (it stands upright); a cup's or pan's lid has a hole for it (a thermometer or spoon goes through the lid). `reads` and `reaches` goals use its reading (°C); a reading taken after its bulb left the water (in_water 0) does not meet `reaches`. Heating and cooling water: a hot-plate (static; 600 W, setpoint_c) heats what stands on it (place {on: <hot plate id>}): a saucepan (water_ml, water_temp_c, lid, salt_g) warms, boils at 100 °C (the temperature stops rising while it boils) and boils away (not with the lid on). A drink-cup (style foam, paper, plastic, glass, steel, mug or flask; water_ml, water_temp_c, lid) of hot water cools through its wall and from its surface (evaporation takes a third to a half of an open cup's heat): a flask or foam with a lid keep it hot longest; an open paper or plastic cup cools fastest (evaporation, and its dull side radiates); a mug's thick cold wall soaks up heat at first; a shiny steel cup radiates little (its outside gets hot to touch), so open it cools about as a foam cup does, and with lids foam keeps it hotter. Without air (settings.air false) nothing evaporates or convects: things cool and melt only by radiation and touch, far slower. An ice cube dropped into a cup melts fast and chills the water. A cold drink-cup (water_temp_c 2-5) in a humid room gets dew on it. Conduction: a spoon (material stainless steel, aluminium, copper, polypropylene (plastic) or varnished hardwood (wood); its bowl at its LEFT end) stood with its bowl end in hot water, or a rod with one end on a hot plate, warms along its length: copper > aluminium > steel > glass > plastic, wood (meltable dabs of butter on it melt where it gets past 33 °C). A meltable is butter (33 °C), chocolate (34 °C) or wax (58 °C). Readings each run (track.state): ice-cube temp, melted (0-1), puddle_g; plate/bowl temp, temp_min; salt-pile salt_g; thermometer reading; drink-cup and saucepan water_temp, water_g, boiling, temp (its wall); hot-plate temp, power; lamp on; spoon and rods temp0 (left end) … temp7 (right end); meltable temp, melted; puddle liquid_g. Fair tests: two identical setups side by side at least 30 cm apart, changing only the one thing compared. Rubbing and impacts warm things (friction's work and the energy an impact loses, half to each side: honest, SMALL sizes): a sanding-block (press_n 5 N, speed 0.5 m/s, rub_s 10 s) on the table warms about +0.1 °C (work_j about 8 J); a 1 kg steel weight dropped 1 m about +0.01 °C. Use goal warms_by {item, at_least_c: 0.05} with time_lapse 1 (the rubbing is real time); never promise a big rise. Candles: the everyday candle with props.lit true (lit_at s) has an 80 W flame 2.5 cm tall that burns 0.1 g of wax a minute (burned_g; it gets lighter, so a kitchen scale under it reads less), gives light (1 candela) and sends hot air up: a thing held 10-20 cm over it warms fast (a bimetal-strip curls, a thermometer reads 50-200 °C). A candle-jar (volume_ml 1000) stood over a SHORT candle (candle height 0.08, mass 0.027; both place {on: table} at the same x, the candle first: the jar is mouth down, not a container to put things inside) traps the air: the flame goes out when its oxygen falls to about 16 % (1 L about 12 s, 2 L about 25 s; goal burns_out {item: candle, jar, before_s?}); the same candle in the open keeps burning. Light that the optics module traces heats what absorbs it: sunlight (sunlight item), a lamp or a flashlight, through a convex-lens, off a mirror or an material-panel (sample aluminium foil), through clear glass (a candle-jar or a clear panel passes about 92 %). A magnifying glass: sunlight from above, a convex-lens (aim 90: its axis up and down) one focal_length above a paper-sheet on the table: its hottest spot (spot_temp) passes 233 °C (goal scorches {item: paper}). Foil reflectors beside an ice cube send it more light (it melts sooner). Liquids: a pitcher (flow module; temp_c, fill_ml) pours into a beaker, measuring-jug, water-tank or bowl: the liquids mix heat for heat (100 g at 80 °C into 100 g at 20 °C gives about 48-50 °C, a little lower for the beaker's own warming); put a thermometer (fixed) in the receiver; goal reaches {item: <receiver or thermometer>, at_least_c} (never at_most_c alone: it is true at the start). Oil, honey, corn syrup and rubbing alcohol in a fluids container warm by their own heat capacity (oil about twice as fast as water; their reading is liquid_temp). A bowl's contents (nothing, water or sand, contents_g, contents_temp_c): dry sand warms about 5 times faster than water under the same lamp (goal warmer {a: sand bowl, b: water bowl}). Solids expand when heated: a ball-and-ring (ball_temp_c 300 sits on the ring until it cools, a cold ball passes; goal passes_through {item, passes?}); a bimetal-strip (layers brass on steel; heated by a lit candle under its tip, a hot plate or start_temp_c, its tip moves about 4 mm a 100 °C for 10 cm; goal bends {item, at_least_mm}). A thermometer's red column rises as its liquid expands with the reading.
  - goal melts {item, by_min?}: the ice cube (or butter, chocolate, wax) melts completely, within by_min minutes of LESSON time (the clock on screen: run seconds × time_lapse ÷ 60; 2 h = 120) if given
  - goal melts_first {a, b}: a melts completely before b (if neither finishes, a has melted more by the end)
  - goal melt_fraction {item, at_least?, at_most?, at_min?}: the share of it melted (0-1) at at_min minutes of lesson time (default the end) is within the bounds
  - goal reaches {item, at_least_c? | at_most_c?, by_min?}: the item's temperature (a thermometer's reading, a cup's or pot's water, else its own) reaches at least at_least_c °C (or cools to at_most_c), within by_min minutes of lesson time if given
  - goal warmer {a, b, at_min?}: a is at least 0.5 °C warmer than b at at_min minutes of lesson time (default the end): which cup kept its drink hotter, which spoon handle got warm
  - goal boils {item, by_min?}: the water in the saucepan, cup or container boils (at 100 °C), within by_min minutes of lesson time if given
  - goal freezes {item, by_min?}: the water in it (a cup, a pot, a puddle) turns all to ice (a room below 0 °C: settings.room_temp −18 is a freezer)
  - goal dries {item, by_min?}: a puddle (or a melted cube's puddle, or the water in a cup or pan) evaporates or boils away, within by_min minutes of lesson time if given (hours: time_lapse 3600)
  - goal dew {item}: water condenses on it (a cold glass or can sweats): it must be colder than the room's dew point (about 11 °C at 22 °C, 50 %)
  - goal burns_out {item, jar?, by_min?, before_s?}: a lit candle's flame goes out (under a candle-jar, named in jar, when its air's oxygen falls to about 16 %: 1 L about 12 s; or its wax is used up)
  - goal scorches {item, by_min?}: focused light (sunlight through a convex-lens, a curved mirror) makes the item's hottest spot pass its scorch point (paper 233 °C, card 260, wood 300)
  - goal passes_through {item, passes?}: a ball-and-ring's ball goes through its ring by the end (passes false: it stays stuck on it); cold it passes, heated (ball_temp_c 300) it sticks until it cools
  - goal bends {item, at_least_mm?}: a bimetal-strip's tip moves at least at_least_mm (default 1) as it heats (about 4 mm a 100 °C for 10 cm)
  - knob candle.lit: only a lit candle gives heat and light (80 W, 0.1 g of wax a minute)
  - knob candle-jar.volume_ml: a bigger jar holds more air (more oxygen), so the candle under it burns longer: about 12 s a litre
  - knob sanding-block.press_n: friction's work grows with how hard it is pressed (μ·N·v): a little more warming
  - knob sanding-block.speed: friction's work grows with the rubbing speed
  - knob sanding-block.rub_s: the longer it is rubbed, the more heat it takes in (it is still small: about 0.01 °C a second)
  - knob ball-and-ring.ball_temp_c: a hotter ball is bigger (brass grows 19 millionths of its size a °C): past about 125 °C it no longer fits the ring
  - knob ball-and-ring.ring_temp_c: a hotter ring has a bigger hole: the hot ball passes again
  - knob bimetal-strip.start_temp_c: its bend grows with how much hotter it is than 20 °C (about 4 mm a 100 °C at the tip of 10 cm)
  - knob bimetal-strip.length: its tip moves as the length squared
  - knob bowl.contents: dry sand (830 J/(kg·K)) warms about 5 times faster than water (4184) under the same lamp
  - knob bowl.contents_g: more water or sand takes longer to warm
  - knob pitcher.temp_c: the mixture lands between the two temperatures, weighted by how much of each
  - knob salt-pile.mass_g: more salt keeps the melt water salty for longer, so the cube melts sooner; the effect is modest (6 g on a 4 cm cube: about 10-20 % sooner) and fades as melt water dilutes it
  - knob salt-pile.grain: fine table salt dissolves about 3 times faster than coarse salt
  - knob ice-cube.width: a smaller cube melts much sooner (its ice grows as size³, its surface as size²): change height and depth with it
  - knob ice-cube.start_temp_c: a colder cube needs more heat first (2 kJ/kg per °C against 334 kJ/kg to melt): a small effect
  - knob lamp.target (a link): only what the beam reaches warms: the lamp must point at the thing it should heat
  - knob lamp.power_w: the heat it gives grows with its power
  - knob lamp.bulb: an incandescent or halogen bulb gives off most of its power as light and heat; an LED gives about a third, almost no heat
  - knob lamp.head_height: a nearer lamp heats much more (1/distance²)
  - knob plate.material: a metal plate feeds a cube heat far faster than ceramic; foam hardly at all
  - knob bowl.material: a metal bowl feeds a cube heat far faster than ceramic; foam hardly at all
  - knob hot-plate.power_w: more power heats what stands on it faster
  - knob hot-plate.setpoint_c: its thermostat holds its top near the setting: a pot boils only when the top is well above 100 °C
  - knob saucepan.water_ml: less water heats (and boils) sooner: it takes 4.2 kJ per kg per °C
  - knob saucepan.lid: a lid keeps steam in: it heats faster and no water boils away
  - knob drink-cup.style: a vacuum flask and foam insulate best; a mug's thick wall soaks up heat at first; an open paper or plastic cup loses most (evaporation and radiation); with no lid the cup matters less than the lid
  - knob drink-cup.lid: a lid stops evaporation, a third to a half of an open hot drink's heat loss
  - knob drink-cup.water_temp_c: where the water starts
  - knob drink-cup.water_ml: more water keeps its temperature longer
  - knob spoon.material: copper and aluminium carry heat along fast, stainless steel slowly, plastic and wood hardly
  - knob steel-rod.material: copper > aluminium > steel > stainless > glass for carrying heat along
  - knob meltable.material: butter melts at about 33 °C, chocolate 34 °C, wax 58 °C
  - knob puddle.water_ml: a smaller puddle dries sooner
  - e.g. "Two ice cubes on white plates; sprinkle salt on one. Which melts first?": two 4 cm ice-cubes each ON its own plate 40 cm apart, a salt-pile (mass_g 6) ON one cube; settings {room_temp 22, time_lapse 600}, seconds 15; goal melts_first {a: salted cube, b: plain cube}
  - e.g. "A big ice cube with salt and a small ice cube without salt, in blue bowls: which melts first?": a 5 cm cube with a salt-pile (6 g) in one bowl (color blue) and a 2.5 cm plain cube in another, time_lapse 900, seconds 12; goal melts_first {a: small, b: big}: size beats salt (not a fair test)
  - e.g. "Shine a desk lamp on one of two salted ice cubes.": two identical cubes with the same salt on identical plates; a lamp (incandescent 60 W) 20 cm to the side of one with props.target = that cube, head_height 0.3; goal melts_first {a: lit cube, b: other}
  - e.g. "An LED lamp versus an old-style bulb on two ice cubes.": two lamps, bulb led and bulb incandescent, each targeting its own cube at the same distance; goal melts_first {a: under the incandescent, b: under the LED}
  - e.g. "Ice cubes on an aluminium plate, a ceramic plate and a foam plate.": three plates (material aluminium, ceramic, foam) 35 cm apart, a 4 cm cube on each, time_lapse 600; goals melts_first {a: aluminium's, b: ceramic's}, melts_first {a: ceramic's, b: foam's}
  - e.g. "Which cup keeps hot cocoa warm longest: foam with a lid, paper, a mug or steel?": four drink-cups (style foam lid true, paper, mug, steel) with 200 mL at 80 °C, a thermometer (fixed) inside each, time_lapse 120, seconds 12 (24 min); goals warmer {a: foam cup, b: steel cup}
  - e.g. "Heat a pot of water on a hot plate until it boils, with a thermometer in it.": hot-plate (600 W), saucepan (1000 mL at 20 °C) ON it, a thermometer (fixed) inside the pot; time_lapse 150, seconds 12 (30 min); goals reaches {item: thermometer, at_least_c: 99}, boils {item: pot}
  - e.g. "Metal spoon or wooden spoon in hot tea: which handle gets warm?": two drink-cups (mug, 90 °C), a spoon (stainless steel) and a spoon (varnished hardwood) each leaning in its mug with its bowl end (left) in the water (angle about 60°, fixed true); time_lapse 60; goal warmer {a: metal spoon, b: wooden spoon}
  - e.g. "Melt butter in a hot pan.": hot-plate (setpoint 150 °C), saucepan with water_ml 0 on it, a meltable (butter) inside the pan; time_lapse 60; goal melts {item: butter}
  - e.g. "Watch a puddle evaporate under a lamp versus in the shade.": two puddles (10 mL) 60 cm apart, a lamp (150 W, head_height 0.25, beam_angle 70) 30 cm to one side of one with props.target = it; time_lapse 3600, seconds 8 (8 h); goals dries {item: lit puddle}, warmer {a: lit puddle, b: other} (the lit one dries in about 5 h, the other keeps about a third of its water)
  - e.g. "A cold drink sweats: water condenses on a glass of ice water.": drink-cup (style glass, water_temp_c 3) in a room at 25 °C (settings.room_temp 25), time_lapse 60, seconds 10; goal dew {item: glass}
  - e.g. "Read the temperature of water with a thermometer.": a drink-cup (glass, 200 mL at 40 °C) and a thermometer (fixed, place inside the cup); seconds 4, time_lapse 30; goal reaches {item: thermometer, at_least_c: 39}
  - e.g. "Does rubbing make things warmer?": a sanding-block on the table (press_n 5, speed 0.5, rub_s 10), seconds 12, time_lapse 1 (real time); goal warms_by {item: block, at_least_c: 0.05}: it warms about 0.1 °C (honest: rubbing warms a little)
  - e.g. "A candle under a jar goes out; one in the open keeps burning.": two short candles (height 0.08, mass 0.027, lit true) 60 cm apart on the table, a candle-jar (volume_ml 1000) on the table at the SAME x as one of them (it stands over it, mouth down); seconds 20; goal burns_out {item: the jar's candle, jar: the jar, before_s: 20}
  - e.g. "Burn paper with a magnifying glass in the sun.": sunlight (elevation 90), a convex-lens (focal_length 0.1, diameter 0.05, aim 90, fixed) 10 cm above a paper-sheet lying on the table; seconds 8; goal scorches {item: paper}
  - e.g. "Mix hot and cold water: what temperature do you get?": a beaker with 200 mL of water at 20 °C and a thermometer (fixed) inside it; a pitcher (vessel cup, fill_ml 200, temp_c 80) with its lip over the beaker, pour_at 1; seconds 15, time_lapse 1; goals reaches {item: beaker, at_least_c: 45} (its water: about 48-50 °C) and reaches {item: thermometer, at_least_c: 40} (it lags)
  - e.g. "Which warms faster in the sun, sand or water?": two bowls (same material) 40 cm apart, contents sand and contents water (contents_g 200), a lamp (incandescent 100 W) 20 cm from each with props.target its bowl; time_lapse 60, seconds 10; goal warmer {a: sand bowl, b: water bowl}
  - e.g. "Show that metal expands when heated (ball and ring).": two ball-and-rings 40 cm apart, one with ball_temp_c 20 and one with ball_temp_c 300; seconds 6; goals passes_through {item: cold one}, passes_through {item: hot one, passes: false}
  - e.g. "A bimetal strip bends over a candle flame.": a bimetal-strip (length 0.1, height 0.12) and a lit candle (height 0.08, mass 0.027) on the table under its tip (candle x = strip x + 0.08); seconds 10, time_lapse 20 (the strip warms over minutes); goal bends {item: strip, at_least_mm: 1.5}
### salt-pile — Salt pile · dynamic
A little cone of table salt. Put it ON an ice cube (resting on its top): it dissolves into the melt water and makes salt water, which melts ice below 0 °C, so the cube melts sooner. More salt keeps the water saltier for longer. On a dry table nothing happens. Facts: 3 g of table salt, 2.7 cm across.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base. Outline at defaults: 0.031 × 0.01 m; from the anchor x −0.015…+0.015, y +0…+0.01.
Props: mass_g: g =3 [0.2…30]; grain: *table* | coarse.
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): salt_g (Salt left, g).
Surface: material table salt; bounce 0.05, friction 0.6, rolling 0.1, side 0.
Notes: also called: salt, table salt, sodium chloride, rock salt, de-icer, sprinkle, melt ice.
### plate — Plate · dynamic
A dinner plate with a low rim. Put an ice cube in its middle: melt water stays on it as a puddle. What it is made of matters: an aluminium plate feeds heat to the cube far faster than ceramic, and foam hardly at all. Facts: 27 cm stoneware dinner plate. Moving parts ≈669 g.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base, where it stands. Outline at defaults: 0.27 × 0.025 m; from the anchor x −0.135…+0.135, y +0…+0.025.
Props: diameter: m =0.27 [0.15…0.32]; color: *white* | blue | red | green | yellow | black | grey | orange | pink | brown.
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): temp (Temperature, °C), temp_min (Coldest spot, °C).
Surface: material *ceramic* | glass | melamine | aluminium | foam | paperboard; bounce 0.484, friction 0.35, rolling 0.002, side 0.
Notes: also called: plate, dish, dinner plate, saucer, ceramic, china, tray, under the ice.
### bowl — Bowl · dynamic
A cereal bowl. An ice cube in it sits in its own melt water (the bowl holds about 5 mm of it round the cube), so salt on the cube stays in contact longer than on a flat plate. Facts: 15 cm stoneware bowl. Moving parts ≈316 g.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base, where it stands. Outline at defaults: 0.15 × 0.065 m; from the anchor x −0.075…+0.075, y +0…+0.065.
Props: diameter: m =0.15 [0.1…0.3]; height: m =0.065 [0.04…0.12]; color: *white* | blue | red | green | yellow | black | grey | orange | pink | brown; contents: *nothing* | water | sand; contents_g: g =200 [10…1000]; contents_temp_c: °C =20 [0…90].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): temp (Temperature, °C), temp_min (Coldest spot, °C).
Surface: material *ceramic* | glass | melamine | aluminium | foam | paperboard; bounce 0.484, friction 0.35, rolling 0.002, side 0.
Notes: container, but NOT usable as a goal container; also called: bowl, dish, cereal bowl, soup bowl, ceramic, basin.
### lamp — Desk lamp · static (fixed in place)
A desk lamp on a heavy base whose shade shines a cone of light and warmth. What its beam reaches warms (an ice cube melts sooner), more the nearer it is (1/distance²). Link it to a target and it points at it. An LED bulb gives light but almost no heat. Facts: 60 W incandescent, shade 40 cm up.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base, where it stands. Outline at defaults: 0.296 × 0.432 m; from the anchor x −0.075…+0.221, y +0…+0.432.
Props: bulb: *incandescent* | halogen | led; power_w: W =60 [1…150]; on: bool =true; on_at: s =0 [0…20]; aim: ° =-60 [-180…180]; beam_angle: ° =100 [40…140]; head_height: m =0.4 [0.2…0.6]; target: link → the id of another item (Aim the beam at this item (its middle)).
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): on (On).
Notes: also called: lamp, desk lamp, light, bulb, heat lamp, incandescent, led, halogen, torch, spotlight.
### thermometer — Thermometer · dynamic
Reads the temperature of what its bulb (the bottom end) is in or touches: water in a cup, a plate, else the air. It takes a while to settle: about 8 s in water and a minute in air for the glass one (3 s and 30 s for the digital probe). In a lamp's beam or the sun it reads high. Tick Fixed to stand it upright in a cup. Facts: glass lab thermometer, −10 to 110 °C. Moving parts ≈36.8 g.
Anchor (x, y): its bulb (the bottom end). Outline at defaults: 0.007 × 0.3 m; from the anchor x −0.0035…+0.0035, y −0.006…+0.294.
Props: style: *glass* | digital; units: *C* | F.
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): reading (Reads, °C), in_water (Bulb in water: 0 no, 1 yes).
Notes: also called: thermometer, temperature, probe, measure, degrees, celsius, fahrenheit, instrument, lab.
### hot-plate — Hot plate · static (fixed in place)
An electric hot plate with an aluminium top 18 cm square. What stands on it (a pot, a beaker, a block) is heated through the touch; its thermostat holds the top near its setting. 600 W brings 1 L of water to the boil in about 10 minutes. Facts: 600 W, set to 250 °C.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base, where it stands. Outline at defaults: 0.2 × 0.086 m; from the anchor x −0.1…+0.1, y +0…+0.086.
Props: power_w: W =600 [100…1500]; setpoint_c: °C =250 [20…550]; on: bool =true; on_at: s =0 [0…20].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): temp (Top, °C), power (Heating, W).
Notes: also called: hot plate, stove, hob, burner, cooker, heater, boil, lab, heat.
### saucepan — Saucepan of water · dynamic
A stainless steel saucepan of water. Stand it on a hot plate: the water warms, boils at 100 °C (the thermometer stops rising while it boils) and boils away; with the lid on, no water is lost. Off the heat it cools, mostly by evaporating from its surface. Facts: 18 cm saucepan, 1 L of water at 20 °C. Moving parts ≈1.98 kg.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base, where it stands. Outline at defaults: 0.306 × 0.103 m; from the anchor x −0.093…+0.213, y +0…+0.103.
Props: diameter: m =0.18 [0.12…0.3]; height: m =0.1 [0.06…0.18]; water_ml: mL =1000 [0…3000]; water_temp_c: °C =20 [0…100]; salt_g: g =0 [0…200]; lid: bool =false.
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): water_temp (Water, °C), water_g (Water left, g), boiling (Boiling), temp (Pan, °C).
Surface: material stainless steel; bounce 0.9, friction 0.4, rolling 0.001, side 0.1.
Notes: container, but NOT usable as a goal container; also called: pot, pan, saucepan, boil, boiling, water, cook, kettle, steam, stove.
### drink-cup — Cup of water · dynamic
A cup of water at a temperature you choose. Hot water cools (cold water warms) through the cup's wall and from its surface: a foam cup with a lid keeps it hot longest after a vacuum flask; an open paper or plastic cup cools fastest; a shiny steel tumbler gets hot to touch but radiates little; an open cup loses a third to a half of its heat by evaporation, which a lid stops. Put a thermometer in it (bulb in the water; it goes through the lid) to read it; drop an ice cube in and it melts and chills the water. Facts: foam cup, 200 mL at 80 °C. Moving parts ≈1.72 g.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base, where it stands. Outline at defaults: 0.09 × 0.107 m; from the anchor x −0.045…+0.045, y +0…+0.107.
Props: style: *foam* | paper | plastic | glass | steel | mug | flask; water_ml: mL =200 [0…500]; water_temp_c: °C =80 [0…100]; lid: bool =false; color: *white* | blue | red | green | yellow | black | grey | orange | pink | brown.
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): water_temp (Water, °C), water_g (Water, g), temp (Cup, °C).
Notes: container, but NOT usable as a goal container; also called: cup, mug, insulated cup, foam cup, styrofoam, thermos, vacuum flask, tumbler, hot chocolate, cocoa.
### spoon — Spoon · dynamic
A spoon (its bowl at its left end). Stand its bowl end in hot water and heat creeps along it: a metal spoon's handle gets warm (copper and aluminium fast, stainless steel slowly), a plastic or wooden one hardly at all. Heat flows along it cell by cell. Facts: 15 cm stainless teaspoon. Moving parts ≈28.8 g.
Anchor (x, y): its middle. Outline at defaults: 0.15 × 0.002 m, centred on the anchor.
Props: length: m =0.15 [0.1…0.35].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): temp0 (Bowl end, °C), temp7 (Handle end, °C), temp (Mean, °C).
Surface: material *stainless steel* | aluminium | copper | polypropylene | varnished hardwood; bounce 0.9, friction 0.4, rolling 0.001, side 0.1.
Notes: also called: spoon, teaspoon, wooden spoon, metal spoon, plastic spoon, conductor, insulator, utensil, stir.
### meltable — Meltable piece (butter, chocolate or wax) · dynamic
A small piece of butter (melts at 32-35 °C), chocolate (34 °C) or candle wax (58 °C). Warm it past that and it melts (it shrinks to a puddle): put dabs along a spoon or a rod to see how far the heat has crept, or chocolate in a lamp's beam or the sun. Facts: a 2 × 1 × 2 cm pat of butter. Moving parts ≈3.64 g.
Anchor (x, y): its centre. Outline at defaults: 0.02 × 0.01 m, centred on the anchor.
Props: width: m =0.02 [0.005…0.1]; height: m =0.01 [0.002…0.05]; depth: m =0.02 [0.005…0.1]; start_temp_c: °C =20 [-20…60].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): temp (Temperature, °C), melted (Melted).
Surface: material *butter* | chocolate | wax; bounce 0.05, friction 0.8, rolling 0.1, side 0.
Notes: also called: butter, chocolate, wax, crayon, melt, dab, pat, conduction race, sun.
### puddle — Puddle of water · dynamic
A puddle of water about 1.5 mm deep. It slowly evaporates (faster when warm, in the sun or a lamp's beam, or in a fan's wind) and thins, its edge staying put, until it is a film that draws in and dries; in a freezing room it freezes. At 22 °C it dries in about 12 h whatever its size (sooner under a lamp): use a time-lapse. Facts: 50 mL puddle, 21 cm across. Moving parts ≈63.5 g.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base. Outline at defaults: 0.206 × 0.0015 m; from the anchor x −0.103…+0.103, y +0…+0.0015.
Props: water_ml: mL =50 [5…1000]; water_temp_c: °C =20 [0…60].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): liquid_g (Water left, g), temp (Temperature, °C).
Surface: material puddle water; bounce 0.05, friction 0.1, rolling 0, side 0.
Notes: also called: puddle, spill, water, evaporate, evaporation, dry, wet, rain.
### sanding-block — Sanding block · dynamic
A small pine block with sandpaper under it that a hand rubs back and forth along what it stands on (a board, the table), pressing down. Friction's work turns to heat in the block and the surface (half each): honest, small sizes, +0.1 °C for 10 s at 5 N and 0.5 m/s (its rubbed face gets much warmer than its mean). A thermometer touching it reads it. Facts: pine 8 × 2.5 × 5 cm, 50 g, pressed with 5 N.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its base (the sandpaper's underside). Outline at defaults: 0.08 × 0.026 m; from the anchor x −0.04…+0.04, y +0…+0.026.
Props: press_n: N =5 [0.5…30]; speed: m/s =0.5 [0.05…1.5]; stroke: m =0.1 [0.02…0.3]; rub_s: s =10 [0.5…30]; rub_at: s =0.5 [0…20].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): temp (Temperature, °C), work_j (Friction's work, J).
Surface: material pine; bounce 0.6, friction 0.45, rolling 0.004, side 0.
Notes: also called: sanding block, sandpaper, rubbing, friction, rub, sand, friction makes heat, warms by rubbing, hands rubbing.
### candle-jar — Jar over a candle · dynamic
A glass jar stood mouth-down on the table (its anchor is the middle of its mouth): put it over a short lit candle (candle height 0.08 m or so, centred under it) and the flame uses up the oxygen in the trapped air and goes out at about 16 %: a 1 L jar in about 10-15 s, a 2 L jar twice as long; the same candle in the open keeps burning. Facts: 1 L glass jar, mouth down. Moving parts ≈287 g.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of its mouth (its rim on the table). Outline at defaults: 0.105 × 0.132 m; from the anchor x −0.053…+0.053, y +0…+0.132.
Props: volume_ml: mL =1000 [250…4000].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): o2_pct (Oxygen inside, %).
Surface: material glass; bounce 0.92, friction 0.4, rolling 0.001, side 0.1.
Notes: also called: jar, glass jar, candle under a jar, oxygen, air, combustion, snuffer, bell jar, candle goes out.
### ball-and-ring — Ball and ring · dynamic, on a fixed frame or pivot (it does not fall)
The classic ball-and-ring: a brass ball dropped onto a steel ring it just passes when cold. Heated (ball_temp_c 300) it is 0.13 mm bigger and sits on the ring until it cools (or heat the ring too: it passes again). The fit is decided by their true sizes, 1 + α·ΔT each (brass 19e-6/K, steel 12e-6/K). Facts: 25.4 mm brass ball, 25.45 mm steel ring. Moving parts ≈72.9 g.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of the stand's base. Outline at defaults: 0.14 × 0.28 m; from the anchor x −0.07…+0.07, y +0…+0.28.
Props: ball_temp_c: °C =20 [-20…600]; ring_temp_c: °C =20 [-20…600]; ball_mm: mm =25.4 [10…50]; hole_mm: mm =25.45 [10…50]; drop: m =0.04 [0…0.2]; ring_height: m =0.2 [0.08…0.4].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): ball_mm (Ball, mm), hole_mm (Hole, mm), fits (Fits), through (Went through), temp (Ball's temperature, °C).
Surface: material brass; bounce 0.6, friction 0.4, rolling 0.002, side 0.
Notes: also called: ball and ring, expansion, thermal expansion, expand, metal expands, heat makes things bigger, gravesande, particles move apart.
### bimetal-strip — Bimetal strip · static (fixed in place)
A strip of brass bonded to steel, clamped at its left end. Heat it (a candle flame under it, a hot plate, a lamp, or start it hot) and it curls toward the steel, because brass expands more: about 4 mm at the tip of a 10 cm strip for 100 °C. A thermostat's or fire alarm's switch. Facts: 10 cm brass-steel strip.
Anchor (x, y): the middle of the stand's base. Outline at defaults: 0.15 × 0.142 m; from the anchor x −0.05…+0.1, y +0…+0.142.
Props: layers: *brass on steel* | steel on brass; length: m =0.1 [0.04…0.2]; height: m =0.12 [0.05…0.3]; start_temp_c: °C =20 [-20…400].
Readings (the run reports them; goals and edits can use them): bend_mm (Tip moves, mm), bend_deg (Bent by, °), temp (Temperature, °C).
Surface: material brass; bounce 0.6, friction 0.4, rolling 0.002, side 0.
Notes: also called: bimetal, bimetallic strip, thermostat, expansion, metal expands, bends when heated, fire alarm.

mod_magnetism.title: Magnets and static electricity
mod_magnetism.text:
### Magnets and static electricity
Magnets (bar-magnet, horseshoe-magnet, disc-magnet, ring-magnets on a dowel, magnet-cart, battery-electromagnet) pull iron and steel and push or pull each other; nothing else is magnetic. Pulled by any magnet: paper-clip (a row of `count` clips), iron-nail, steel-washer, steel-can, can-on-side with material steel, clip-on-thread, the catalog's steel balls and steel weights, and the other modules' iron and steel (the matter module's steel density cube and steel wool, cast iron, a cart's steel spring bumper). NOT pulled at all: plastic-clip, foil-ball, copper-wire, brass-key, wooden-bead, coins (a penny is copper-plated zinc), aluminium cans, stainless-steel spoons and pans (austenitic), the density set's aluminium, brass, copper and zinc cubes, glass, wood, plastic, rubber. (A cart's magnet bumpers are magnets of their own: not modelled as iron.) Poles: a bar magnet's north (red, N) is on its right (+x) unless `flip`; turn it with its angle (angle_deg -90 points its north pole DOWN, 90 up). Like poles facing push apart, unlike pull together; iron is pulled by either pole. Strength: `material` ceramic (B_r 0.39 T) < alnico (1.07 T working) < neodymium (1.3 T): at the same size neodymium pulls about 11 times harder than ceramic at contact. Distance matters a lot: the pull falls off steeply (two magnets far apart as 1/distance⁴; a magnet on a clip faster). A 15 cm ceramic bar held pole-down lifts a paper clip lying on the table from about 1.5 cm below it, a neodymium bar from about 3 cm; lying on the table end-on, a clip slides to a ceramic bar's pole from 3 cm, to a neodymium one from 5 cm. Hold (`fixed: true`) a magnet that should stay where it is (above clips, in front of a row of objects); leave carts and things to be pulled free. A barrier-sheet between a magnet and a clip: paper, cardboard, plastic, glass and aluminium change nothing; a steel one (0.5 mm) blocks most of a ceramic magnet's pull (a clip 8 mm behind it stays put) but a neodymium bar saturates it and still pulls about half. magnet-cart: a wooden cart with a bar magnet on its deck (`magnet_end` front/back, `flip`). Two carts 5-10 cm apart with like poles facing (one flipped or its magnet at the back facing the other's front with flip) roll apart; unlike poles roll together. ring-magnets: `count` rings on an upright dowel; with `alternate` (like faces together) each ring floats where the push equals the weight above it (the bottom gap smaller); unlike faces snap together. compass: stands face-on, its needle's red end points north (right, unless `north` left: it starts that way) by the Earth's field (`earth`), and near a magnet lines up with its field: red end toward the magnet's south pole and away from its north; a magnet flipped right in line with it swings it round. Its needle always turns on its pivot, a fixed (held) compass's too. Its reading heading_deg is the red end's direction, counter-clockwise from the right (0 right, 90 up, 180 left). battery-electromagnet: a nail wrapped with `turns` of wire on `cells` AA batteries, held point down (fixed); switched `on` (at `on_at` s) it is a magnet: it picks up a clip lying 0.5-1 cm under its point, and holds a chain of clips hung from its point (paper-clip count 6, spacing 0.0345, angle -90, held: the ones it cannot hold fall at the release; on 2 AA, 10 turns hold one, 50 two, 200 three: a chain end to end holds few, as a real one does). More turns make it stronger until the nail's iron is full (about 300 turns); more batteries add little current with few turns (the batteries' own resistance limits it to about 6 A). It has its own batteries: the circuits module has no coil to wire it into a circuit, so switch it with `on` and `on_at`. Static electricity: a balloon `rubbed` N strokes (on hair or wool) carries −10 nC a stroke up to −100 nC on its `rubbed_side` (bottom, top, left, right, lower right, lower left); hung `on_thread` from a hook (its `thread` length) it swings. It pulls paper-bits (light, polarized: they stand up and jump to it from about 1 cm below its rubbed side) and an aluminium can-on-side (rolls toward it from a few cm). Two rubbed balloons hung 30 cm apart with rubbed sides facing push apart (they swing apart about 5-10°). Any light thing that is not metal is polarized as a dielectric (its ε_r: paper 2-3, plastic 2-3.5, wood 1.4-2.7, water 80): a ping-pong ball rolls to a rubbed balloon only from about 5 mm (a plastic shell is weakly polarized), where an aluminium can goes from several cm; other modules' metals (a penny, a spoon) are conductors. charged-rod (fixed: plastic rubbed with wool negative, glass with silk positive) and pith-ball (a light conductor on a thread: pulled, touches, takes some charge and is pushed away). Readings each run: pull_mN (the magnetic or electric force on the item now), magnetized (%, soft iron), amps (an electromagnet's current), heading_deg (a magnet's or compass needle's north end), charge_uC (a charged item's charge). Field lines are a drawing option (`show_field` on a magnet). For a picture of a paper-clip, plastic-clip, clip-on-thread or steel-washer (a thin sliver from the side): `facing` face-on stands it on its edge, its face toward the camera (the same steel and weight; its side outline is then its face: a clip 33 × 8 mm, a washer its ring).
  - goal attracts {source, item}: the source (a magnet, a charged balloon or rod) pulls the item to it: the item starts more than 3 mm from it (one that starts touching was not pulled: use sticks) and ends touching it, or 1 cm or more nearer than it started
  - goal repels {a, b, min_m?}: a and b push each other apart: the gap between them grows by min_m (default 1 cm) or more at its widest (hung balloons swing apart and back)
  - goal sticks {item, to}: the item touches `to` (within 3 mm) all through the run's last half second
  - goal lifts {source, item, min_m?}: the item rises at least min_m (default 5 mm) and ends nearer the source (a clip jumping up to a magnet held above it)
  - goal points {compass, toward? | angle_deg?, tol_deg?}: the compass needle's red (north) end ends pointing at the item's middle, or along angle_deg (0 right, 90 up, 180 left), within tol_deg (default 15)
  - goal holds {magnet, count, items?}: at least `count` pieces of iron or steel (clips, nails, washers: every soft-iron item's pieces, or those of `items`) end hanging from the magnet: touching it or a piece that does, and touching nothing else (off the table)
  - goal levitates {item, count?, min_m?}: ring magnets: at least count rings (default all but the bottom one) float with a gap of min_m (2 mm) under each; anything else: it ends in the air (min_m, default 1 cm, above the table) touching nothing of another item (a clip on a thread under a magnet)
  - goal not_attracted {source, item, max_m?}: the item is NOT pulled to the source: all through the run it never comes more than max_m (default 3 mm) nearer to it than it started. Use it for every test object that must stay put (the plastic clip, foil, brass key, wooden bead next to a magnet; the paper under an unrubbed balloon)
